headline: Record-breaking sightings of rare moth in Essex
body:
Fisher's estuarine moths are highly threatened due to coastal erosion

Wildlife enthusiasts have made a record-breaking number of sightings of an elusive moth at a nature reserve.

The Fisher's estuarine moth has been spotted 111 times at Abbotts Hall in Great Wigborough, near Colchester, in 2026.

Dr Zoe Ringwood, of Essex Wildlife Trust, said work to boost the highly threatened species' population had been an "important success story".

The charity has pledged to continue surveying new and existing plots on the Essex coast.

Fisher's estuarine moths can be recognised by their pale gold-brown wing colour with light and dark spots, and are naturally found in low-lying areas of natural grassland which are vulnerable to erosion.

They are reliant on rare hog's fennel for their survival, but the plant has been affected by rising sea levels.

To protect the species, Essex Wildlife Trust planted hog's fennel at Abbotts Hall in 2005 and introduced moth eggs five years later.

There is now a self-sustaining population of the moth at Abbotts Hall, according to Essex Wildlife Trust

More than 100 of the scarce insect were recorded for the first time in 2025, before the record was broken again in 2026.

The charity said it was confident there was now a self-sustaining population at Abbotts Hall.

"[It is] a reflection of how taking evidence-based conservation action can achieve positive results for a threatened Essex species," said Ringwood, its senior conservation evidence manager.

headline: Man charged with attempted murder after Bradford councillor stabbed
body:
Councillor Ibrar Ali remains in a serious but stable condition in hospital

A man has appeared in court charged with attempted murder after a Bradford councillor was seriously injured in a stabbing.

Councillor Ibrar Ali was attacked at about 11:00 GMT on Thursday on Thornbury Avenue, before being driven to nearby Manse Street, according to West Yorkshire Police.

Arfan Ali, 32, of Thornbury Avenue, is also charged with assault and possession of an offensive weapon in a public place. At Leeds Magistrates' Court earlier, he was remanded into custody until he appears at Bradford Crown Court on 21 December.

Councillor Ali remains in hospital in a serious but stable condition, police said.

Councillor Ali is a Your Bradford Independent Group representative for Bradford Moor ward and was first elected in May.

He works as a community development manager at charity The Leap, and was one of the founders of Leeds Road Festival.

Speaking after Thursday's incident, his family thanked police, paramedics and members of the public who "courageously provided first aid and assistance at the scene" and asked people to "keep him and his family in your duas [prayers]".

headline: Birth excitement 'turns to worry' over maternity move
body:
Shelly Magee and Clinton McKeever had hoped their son would be born in Newry

A couple who are expecting their first child have said their excitement has turned "into complete worry" because of the suspension of maternity services at their local hospital.

Shelly Magee was due to give birth in Newry's Daisy Hill Hospital in January but from Monday, the Southern Trust is moving all hospital-based births to Craigavon.

Her partner, Clinton McKeever, said they are now dreading the much longer journey from their home in Mullaghbawn to Craigavon in the middle of winter.

The trust announced the temporary suspension of maternity services at Daisy Hill in September, saying it had been unable to recruit enough consultant obstetricians to maintain a safe service for both mums and babies.

From Monday, it has advised all expectant mothers in the Southern Health Trust to go to Craigavon Area Hospital - not Daisy Hill - for all labour and birthing services, inpatient maternity care and emergency gynaecology support.

The trust said an estimated 13 women could possibly deliver their babies on Monday at Craigavon.

That includes planned C sections and those booked in for induction - four of these had originally planned to have their babies in Daisy Hill.

It added that patients will receive the same high standard of care from experienced specialists, including staff from Daisy Hill who are relocating to Craigavon.

But the expectant couple have not been reassured by the trust's statements.

Magee said Craigavon Area Hospital is "50 minutes from the house" by car but her partner pointed out that could rise to 90 minutes in heavy traffic or severe weather.

"A child doesn't choose a time to come," McKeever told BBC News NI.

"To strip away a maternity service and claim it's for the safety of women is scandalous... there's no thought of safety in that journey."

He said he was speaking from experience, having "had a taste of the journey already in a scenario that would be considered a crisis".

About five years ago, his father was badly injured in a fall during which he suffered several broken ribs and a punctured lung.

McKeever drove his father to Craigavon, having been advised by their local health clinic that it would take too long for an ambulance to get to Mullaghbawn.

"The traffic was crazy and he felt every bump - I felt guilty for every bump. I got him there in the end but it was a very, very stressful journey," he recalled.

"To know that I have to do it again with Shelly here, it's very concerning. It's took the excitement out of the whole thing and turned it into complete worry."

To avoid having to drive to Craigavon in active labour in early January the couple are now considering booking a hotel or rented accommodation near the hospital.

Despite their concerns, they were full of praise for midwives who cared for them in Newry and Crossmaglen, acknowledging staff also face uncertainty.

"They're brilliant, they keep up with everything, but they're in the dark as much as we are, that's the frustrating thing," Magee said.

The trust apologised to women who had planned to give birth at Daisy Hill Hospital

Hospital campaigners have also raised concerns about what the trust is describing as a temporary suspension.

Conor Patterson, chair of the Daisy Hill Future Group, expressed "deep concern" that the move would affect "time-critical access to maternity care".

He claimed it subjects families in counties Down, Armagh and the border area to "life and death risks".

"Moving up to 1,800 births from Newry to Craigavon risks not just destabilising Craigavon's maternity unit but will threaten also its ability to safely provide other acute medical services."

According to figures from the trust, 1,713 babies were born at Daisy Hill last year, while Craigavon dealt with 2,768 births.

When asked how Craigavon will deal with hundreds of extra births each year, the trust said it was continuing efforts to secure consultant obstetricians for Daisy Hill. There are also plans to open an additional ward.

It said it was also preparing continuity arrangements to temporarily consolidate births and inpatient maternity care at Craigavon from Monday.

The trust employs 15 consultant obstetricians. However, sickness, reduced working hours and maternity leave means not all 15 can contribute to the on-call rota.

Despite ongoing recruitment efforts across the UK and internationally, the trust said it has been unable to recruit enough consultants to maintain a safe and reliable service at both hospitals.

Its spokesperson said inpatient maternity care at Craigavon had been identified as the safest and most sustainable arrangement for maintaining the trust's services.

The number of midwives employed within the maternity units at both acute hospitals has dropped from pre-pandemic levels.

In October 2019, there were 55.6 midwives employed on a full-time basis at Daisy Hill Hospital and 95.04 full-time in Craigavon.

As of last month, that had dropped to 47.57 midwives at Daisy Hill and 82.58 in Craigavon.

However, the trust said midwifery care has changed over the past seven years, with more midwives now working in the community.

The trust added that 16 newly-appointed midwives are due to start work between November 2026 and January 2027.

Its medical director for maternity and women's health, Dr Beverley Adams, said all efforts had been made to avoid the suspension and she apologised for any disappointment caused for women who had planned to give birth at Daisy Hill.

"Teams at both hospitals have been working hard to manage these challenges and prepare to provide all births, inpatient maternity care and emergency gynae care for the Southern Trust at Craigavon Area hospital."

A spokesperson for the trust said that of the 1,088 planned births up to the end of February, it estimated that 294 of these were originally planned for Daisy Hill.

A proportion of these women may already have been referred to Craigavon based on risk.

To support the maternity service at Craigavon, a total of 37 staff, including midwives and sisters, are to transfer.

It is not the first time that Daisy Hill has lost hospital services because of staffing problems.

Its emergency general surgery was permanently moved to Craigavon in 2024, two years after it was temporarily suspended due to recruitment challenges.

headline: Wildlife conservation cash targets ex-colliery sites
body:
The project aims to create and restore habitats for amphibians and lizards

Ponds are to be restored and freshwater habitats created for amphibians and reptiles at two former colliery sites in South Yorkshire.

The Froglife charity has been awarded nearly £890,000 of Lottery cash to carry out the work in Rother Valley, as well as at sites in North and West Yorkshire.

Kiveton and Dinnington Community Woodlands were originally regenerated through the National Coalfields Programme after the pits there closed in the 1990s.

Sheila Grundry, from Froglife, said staff were "delighted" to work in the area because "freshwater will make a lasting difference for frogs and other wildlife and it's a great way for local people to learn new skills".

The £889,761 investment in Froglife's Coalface to Wildspace project will also help local communities connect with nature, according to the charity.

Dinnington Woodland is one of the sites in Yorkshire which will be a focus of the project

The aim of the project across Yorkshire is to create 48 new ponds, improve 93 existing freshwater habitats and establish new "neighbourhood wildlife corridors" like small ponds and bug hotels.

These "corridors" will act as stepping stones for local wildlife from insects to birds, providing food, shelter and water to improve biodiversity across former industrial sites and help wildlife move between one habitat and another.

Conservationist Andy Goff, project manager in Yorkshire, said the transformation of the sites would be for everyone.

"These former industrial sites are an important part of our area's history," he said.

"This project will help transform them into thriving habitats while creating opportunities for local people to get involved."

headline: New charity uses outdoors to improve mental health
body:
Kate Bergquist said the outdoors needed to be recognised as a form of healthcare

A new charity hopes to use activities ranging from cold-water swimming and archery to hill walking and breathwork to improve men's mental health and reduce isolation.

Connect Outdoors is being officially launched alongside an International Men's Day event at the Venture Centre in Maughold, where organisers expect about 80 people to take part in a range of outdoor activities.

The charity said it wanted to gather research on what kind of support men are most likely to engage with, arguing that services have often been designed without asking men first.

Chief executive Kate Bergquist said it had grown out of years of work in social care, public services and outdoor wellbeing programmes.

She said: "We have this abundance of landscape on the island that is never used enough for health.

"This should be embedded into everyone's health and wellbeing routine every week."

Activities on offer include high ropes, bushcraft, mindfulness, breathwork, yoga, archery, ice baths and guided walks, alongside informal spaces designed to encourage men to connect with one another.

The charity is built around what is known as "green and blue health", which encourages people to use natural environments such as forests, beaches and the sea to improve their health.

Bergquist said a key focus would be addressing men's mental health through activities that encourage conversation without making mental health the main selling point.

As part of Sunday's event, attendees will be invited to complete surveys that organisers hope will help identify which activities and approaches are most effective at engaging men.

Among those supporting the event is Gary Thomas, who runs Walking for Wellness and takes people on Manx hill walks where they can talk through any challenges.

Gary Thomas said being in nature helped people to feel less isolated

The former serviceman and mountain leader said many people found it easier to open up outdoors than in a traditional counselling setting.

"It gives them that opportunity to feel secure and have that ability to open up in an environment that's not oppressive," he said.

"Nature's not clinical, nature's natural."

Thomas said group activities could also help tackle loneliness by creating new social connections.

"We've had people turn up and find their own circle of friends and common interests," he said.

"Then they go off afterwards and explore things together, which is brilliant."

Also involved in the event is Douglas barber Joshua Moore, who completed suicide prevention training through the Lions Barber Collective.

Joshua Moore said the barber's chair was a "special place" for people to open up

Moore runs Renegade: Cuts and Clobber, and said barber shops often became places where men felt comfortable discussing difficult issues.

"The barber chair is a very special place," he said.

"You can leave feeling a little bit better about yourself, whether that's having a nice haircut, but also just having the opportunity for somebody to listen to you."

Moore said he had seen first-hand the impact mental health struggles could have on families and communities, and wanted to support initiatives aimed at encouraging conversation and early intervention.

The International Men's Day event aimed to introduce men to new activities and point participants to support available to improve both their physical and mental wellbeing.

headline: Why Gen Z are planning for life without a state pension
body:
Joel has finally landed his first graduate engineering job after several years of lower‑paid roles. He's in his early 20s, lives with his parents and works in London. But instead of splashing the extra cash, or saving up for holidays or a house deposit, he's decided to squirrel more of it away into his workplace pension.

The reason? He doesn't think he'll get any kind of state pension. Like Joel, around half of Gen Z (those born from 1997–2012) say they don't expect the state pension to exist by the time they retire. It's pretty stark to hear, but growing up with constant headlines about an ageing population, a proportionally smaller working-age population, and the pressure that government finances are under, Joel thinks it's his generation that will suffer.

"I don't believe that I'll be a recipient of a state pension. I know a lot of people my age don't think they're going to be... There just won't be enough money," he says.

Retirement has always felt distant when you're in your 20s - something to think about later. But what's emerging among today's under‑30s is something different: not just distance, but doubt.

"It just mathematically doesn't make sense… There has to get to a point where that state pension is taking up too much of the budget and can't exist in the way that it exists right now," Joel says.

"I don't believe that I'll be a recipient of a state pension," says Joel

The state pension age is shifting. At the start of April, the age at which you receive it began to gradually creep up, rising from 66 years to 67 years by March 2028. It's due to go up again in 20 years' time to 68, though that might happen earlier as the government has an ongoing independent review.

That's a frustration for 27-year-old retail manager Connor, who got in touch via BBC Your Voice, because he says "the goalpost keeps moving". "At the minute I'll be 68 by the time I can retire, but I do think I'll be probably closer to 75, if I'm honest."

More than 13 million people - 19% of the population - are currently of state pension age. By 2050, even with the state pension age rising to 68, that group is projected to exceed 15 million people, nearly a quarter of the population, with numbers projected to climb towards 17 million by the 2070s. In other words, there will be lots more people qualifying for the state pension, and fewer working people, as a proportion, paying taxes into the pot to cover the bill.

At the same time, almost half of working‑age adults are not paying into a private pension pot. That means many will be relying solely on the state pension for their retirement income - and with relative poverty rates among pensioners now at 14%, we can already see how difficult that can be.

Experts warn that if a whole generation stops believing the state pension will be there, it could push people towards more risky investments, prompt overly restrictive behaviour, or lead others not to save at all.

So, are we heading towards a major pension crisis for many in Gen Z? And if we are, might the Gen Z generation end up redefining what retirement looks like?

For those hitting the state pension milestone today, as long as they've made 35 years of National Insurance contributions, they're entitled to £241.30 a week.

That amount rises each year to help people keep pace with rising living costs. Since 2011, pension increases have been guaranteed by the triple lock - which means the rise will either match the rate of inflation, average earnings or 2.5% - whichever is higher.

But in recent weeks, several organisations have called for the rules to be rewritten.

The centre-left Resolution Foundation think tank has argued for scrapping the triple lock, saying that continuing to prioritise the incomes of pensioners over working-age adults and children would be unfair.

Meanwhile, the Tony Blair Institute (TBI), a think tank set up by the former prime minister, takes things a step further and has called for the whole state pension to be scrapped and replaced with a new "Lifespan Fund". Thomas Smith, director of economic policy at the TBI, argued: "Britain's state pension system was built for a different era. We can't keep pouring money into a system that is increasingly unaffordable."

It suggests scrapping the triple lock and allowing people to access some of their state pension early if they need it because of redundancy and frequent job changes.

That's an idea that might appeal to Connor in Chesterfield. He's facing redundancy from his job at a global cosmetics firm, and the ability to draw down a small amount - effectively a withdrawal from his future state pension - might tide him through.

"There's not that many jobs out there at the minute, unfortunately. I still live at home with my parents luckily, but I pay board to them. I still have a car payment, I still have my insurance to pay."

"There's not that many jobs out there," says Connor

But former pensions minister Steve Webb argues those changes would be "a huge backward step". He says the benefit of the current system is its simplicity which shouldn't be replaced with "something fiendishly complex and highly intrusive, which would take many decades to implement in full."

The government says it has committed to the triple lock for the rest of this parliament, and that the Pensions Commission, an independent body set up to review the regime for UK private pensions, is examining "how we can ensure secure retirements for tomorrow's pensioners".

It's likely that those in their 20s will not have a triple‑locked pension. That means living on the state pension alone will become more difficult, as its value may rise more slowly than the cost of food, travel, clothing and household bills.

For those who doubt the triple lock will endure, the debate often shifts to how the state pension can be sustained at all. One idea that regularly surfaces is means‑testing. In some ways it already is: very low‑income pensioners can receive an additional benefit called Pension Credit. But 24‑year‑old Joel believes that for the state pension to survive, the choices may need to be more radical.

"I don't think a means-tested state pension is necessarily a bad thing. But it would be a bad thing if it only applies to people in 50 years and not now when we should be saving some of that money."

Engineer Joel is one of life's squirrels. His fear about the future of the state pension means he's doubling-down on his private pension. He contacted BBC Your Voice because he feels that consecutive governments have sheltered current pensioners, leaving the consequences for his generation to face.

"I'm going to have to increase the amount of my paycheck that goes into a private pension, which obviously isn't good with cost of living through the roof," he says.

The scale of what younger workers may need to save adds to that anxiety for some. Investment company Rathbones estimates that a single person retiring today at 65 (with the state pension) may need around £796,000 in savings to fund a "comfortable retirement". If the state pension remains, a 25‑year‑old today would need a pot of around £1.68m to retire comfortably as a single person. Without the state pension, the figure for Gen Z jumps to more than £2.4m.

Against this backdrop, Joel says many of his friends are considering opting out of private and workplace pensions altogether and investing independently instead, mostly in "crypto or index funds and things like that.

"There's a sense, whether it's right or wrong, that that's more secure than putting it in a pension where they're also going to take a chip on top."

It's possible that individual investment choices could earn more than a pension scheme, but it's a big gamble.

Behavioural economics suggests that when people lose trust in a system, they tend to either opt out entirely or over‑compensate. Both can be problematic. Saving extra in a private pension may limit current life options, but opting out can leave many with riskier retirement savings, or indeed none at all.

In central Manchester, 23‑year‑old Ashleigh agrees with Joel that the state pension is unlikely to be coming her way: "At this rate I don't think anyone's ever going to retire, I think everyone will just have to fend for themselves in the end."

But as someone on a lower income, her pension choices are less squirrel‑like. When working for a big retailer, she says that she chose to stop contributing to her employer's auto-enrolment pension.

"I opted out of it. I need the money now." She explains: "I'd rather save for a house and then at least I have something to show for it".

Some experts warn that the gap between rich and poor in retirement could widen significantly for this generation.

Dr Suzy Morrissey, deputy director at the Pensions Policy Institute (PPI), believes that alongside how much Gen Z save privately, another factor will widen the divide: far more of them will be renting.

"Renting in retirement increases your chances of pensioner poverty, and they do face challenges to save, as younger people, that previous generations didn't face when they were at the same age," she says. "If we have people paying rent in retirement who don't have large pension pots to cover those expenses, then that equals higher risk of pensioner poverty."

But Morrissey sees a silver lining: pensions auto-enrollment, the system that automatically puts most employees into a workplace pension unless they opt out. If they've been employees, "they will have spent their working life contributing into a pension pot, and they will be the first generation that will have spent their whole life doing that."

It'll be a backstop for many, but the minimum contribution rate is unlikely to be enough for a comfortable retirement. It's not automatic for the self-employed and people like Ashleigh have opted out because of immediate financial pressures, so it looks like plenty won't see the benefit of that silver lining.

For some, the response to an uncertain future is to focus on the present.

Lauren, from Hull, says: "Money always comes back, time doesn't. The world is so vast, we shouldn't wait till the last 10/20 years of our lives to go out and see it!"

At 24, she's about to take six months off from her job as a business coordinator. She's one of a growing number planning to take regular career breaks, or "grown-up gap years", which many are terming "mini retirement". HSBC's 2025 UK survey found that 63% of Gen Z plan to take at least one mini‑retirement, compared with 32% of Gen X and 13% of Boomers.

"The majority of my friends don't pay into pensions and instead decide to take their whole wage [after taxes] and spend it how they see fit. A large proportion goes on travels or holidays," says Lauren.

"I currently don't pay into a pension, actually I never have. I'd way rather have my money now and use it to live life," she says.

"The majority of my friends don't pay into pensions," says Lauren

But there's a warning for Gen Z from the experience of the Waspi women - hundreds of thousands born in the 1950s who campaigners say have suffered because of poorly communicated rises in the state pension age. Their financial shock shows that costs may only become clear when it's too late to course-correct.

If Gen Z's suspicions are right, and the state pension becomes a less dependable part of income in later life, then more will have to take a totally different approach to retirement, savings and life choices to navigate the new landscape.

headline: Can AI really help spot Black Friday deals? We put it to the test
body:
Whether it's scrolling through endless choice, spotting fake reviews, or working out if a "deal" is a deal at all, Black Friday sums up a lot of online woes.

Retailers promise bargains - but the sheer number of offers can leave us feeling no closer to finding the best deal.

It's an area where generative AI products, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, have promised to help.

But are they any good at finding Black Friday deals? We had a go ourselves a week ahead of the big day.

Figures suggest relatively few UK shoppers currently go to AI tools for help.

A recent YouGov survey of 19 countries found the UK ranked second-last in the proportion of people who said they had used AI to help them shop.

Crucially, 36% of respondents who said they would be shopping around Black Friday didn't plan to use an AI tool at all.

But the survey suggested a growing number of people were considering it - and tech firms have released features to capitalise on this.

Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping for UK users in November and OpenAI launched a Shopping Research tool on ChatGPT days before last year's Black Friday.

In the US, Google recently launched Universal Cart, with AI-powered features such as price tracking and identification of relevant promo codes.

But there has been criticism that fact-checking AI ends up taking more time, while some brands are working to try to make sure their products show up in chatbot answers.

Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping for UK users in November and OpenAI launched a Shopping Research tool on ChatGPT days before last year's Black Friday.

In the US, Google recently launched Universal Cart, with AI-powered features such as price tracking and identification of relevant promo codes.

But there has been criticism that fact-checking AI ends up taking more time, while some brands are working to try to make sure their products show up in chatbot answers.

We asked four models to find a 55-inch TV deal, using the free versions of many of the most popular tools.

While this was not a rigorous scientific test, the experience we had produced mixed results.

OpenAI's ChatGPT came up with four options.

Its top pick was a Hisense TV on Chinese retailer Joybuy's website, on sale for £499 down from £649.

The next recommendation was a 55-inch TCL-branded TV, but a sidebar showed prices for the 50-inch version, from £379 to £814.

Option three was the same Hisense TV as before, but for full price at £649 from John Lewis and Richer Sounds.

This was the "best safer purchase" according to ChatGPT, as the sites offered longer guarantee periods.

But clicking on the links did not go well. Both retailers said the TV was no longer listed online.

The fourth option was equally fruitless - another TCL TV, at full price, £150 over our budget and not available online.

At the bottom, ChatGPT served one last offer - "one OLED option to compare" - for a £1,100 LG TV that was marked as "Ad".

Claude produced the shortest answer of all the models we tested, and unlike the others, it did not give much detail on the specifications of each model.

Instead, it seemed to base its results on a small number of reviews published online.

It recommended the same two TCL TVs as ChatGPT.

But when we clicked on the links, they sent us to two dead pages on the Richer Sounds website.

Some other links led to year-old round-ups of Black Friday 2025 deals.

Claude was not very enthusiastic about its other two recommendations due to a lack of independent reviews - calling one "a decent option" but saying it "wouldn't pick" the other.

It also listed two Samsung TVs, but it told us not to buy them, with one "over budget and not clearly better than the TCLs".

We were left wondering why it even mentioned them in the first place.

Different AI model, same TV manufacturers - albeit different Hisense and TCL models to the previous chatbots' recommendations.

Gemini generated a table comparing four different models, but offered no links to the stores it named, so we searched for them ourselves.

The prices for one TCL TV were correct at £649, but it was sold out at one of the named retailers.

It said the other TCL model was available from Argos and Currys for £539 - correct for Argos, but when we checked Currys, it was £60 more expensive.

Again, it included two Samsung models to avoid due to lower screen specs.

Alexa came back with four TVs, from its own Amazon Ember at £532 to a £699 Samsung.

But its top recommendation was to go for another Samsung model at £616 (down from £749), based on its picture quality and Amazon customer rating.

Its fourth option was for a Sony TV, but it was only 50 inches, leaving us unsure why it had included it.

All the prices stated were correct, but Amazon only searches its own store. Alexa did acknowledge this, encouraging us to check its rivals for better deals, "as prices can vary" and we could get longer guarantees elsewhere.

There are methods that can boost the likelihood of getting a better response, from crafting more informative prompts to upping a chatbot's "thinking" level.

Tech journalist Alex Hughes had better luck than we did when he used ChatGPT's agentic AI mode to find a TV in last year's Black Friday sales.

Agentic AI is still in its early days, but it allows AI to act with more autonomy and carry out multi-step tasks.

The search took about 20 minutes "with very little work on my end needed," Hughes wrote for Tom's Guide, external in November 2025.

A year on, he told the BBC he didn't go through with buying a TV at that time.

He did later purchase one of the seven models ChatGPT had surfaced - but he had found it for a lower price in a bricks-and-mortar shop.

Will he be using AI to find Black Friday deals again this year? "Probably not," he said.

He reckoned it saved him time, but "when you're trying to deal with something like live price data... it will be inconsistent and quite often incorrect".

While we were served up the same brands again and again, in reality there are tonnes of products listed for sale around Black Friday.

Naureen Mohammed, who advises businesses on how to get their products to appear in AI results, told the BBC customers did not see the full picture when they talked to chatbots.

If businesses fail to update their prices when people start hunting for bargains, "last year's prices are served up as today's deals".

"I suspect the whole model for advertising is going to start influencing AI recommendations," she said.

Her own analysis of chatbots' Black Friday tech deals in the UK suggested the big retailers came out on top - with Amazon mentioned in half of responses, and Currys following closely behind.

Her tips include asking an assistant "is that this year's price?" and clicking on the links provided - "because you shouldn't take any advice from the AI system at face value".

But consumer group Which? recently said inaccurate pricing in AI results added more work, external to Black Friday deal-hunting.

"If you ask ChatGPT for a list of 10 laptops under £400 and seven of the results are priced higher, you've likely wasted a good chunk of time going through them to discover the bot gave you only three options," said senior researcher Hannah Walsh.

"The opposite is also true - you could miss out on great models in your budget if ChatGPT tells you they are more expensive than they actually are."

headline: Anthropic raises $81bn in record-breaking stock market debut
body:
Watch: How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold?

Anthropic, the company behind AI chatbot Claude, has raised a record $81bn (£62bn) in a stock market debut that will make it one of the most valuable companies in the world.

A surge of investor appetite to buy shares in the loss-making business meant more stock was sold than originally planned. Anthropic's shares have been priced at $83, up from the proposed $70-$78 range.

Shares will begin trading later on Thursday in New York, valuing the five year-old firm at around $1.5 trillion.

The flotation is being seen as a crucial test for fast-growing AI sector. Anthropic is the first purely AI-focused firm to publicly sell its shares.

Vast amounts of money have been poured into AI infrastructure and the development of AI based tools. But questions are being raised over whether and when those investments will pay off.

The seven founders, who set up Anthropic up in 2021, will become multi-billionaires immediately.

The company's $1.5tn estimated valuation is on a "diluted" basis, a broader reflection of the firm's value that takes things like employee stock options into account. On a basic share count Anthropic is worth about $1.1tn, more valuable than Walmart and Samsung but less than Tesla and Meta.

But strong demand could push its share price, and overall valuation, higher, once shares are publicly traded.

But strong demand could push its share price, and overall valuation, higher, once shares are publicly traded.

One early investor in the company who spoke to the BBC on condition of anonymity, said the original sale was heavily oversubscribed, with demand ten times the number of shares available.

Anthropic's revenues have ballooned in the last year, to $33bn in the nine months to September this year, as the market for its tools, designed to speed up processes including coding, writing and digesting information, has grown.

But net losses have also increased, reaching $104bn for the same period, according to the company's IPO document.

Leah Bramwell from Canaccord Wealth said there had been strong interest in Anthropic shares "across the board" including both institutional and retail - that is private individual - investors, which she said suggested it was not simply a "retail-driven frenzy into into AI names".

In total Anthropic could raise $107bn. Over $81bn comes from the public share sale, with an additional $26bn from separate investments from a group of tech firms including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.

Anthropic could raise a further $12bn through an additional provision, which is normal practice, to permit further shares to be sold if demand is very high.

Elon Musk's SpaceX raised an initial $75bn in its IPO in June this year.

The company soared in value when it joined the Nasdaq, reaching $2.2tn, although in the weeks that followed, the share price fell.

Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei co-founded firm five years ago

OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest AI rival, is expected to go public next year. Until then, Anthropic will be the only public company in the US that is entirely focused on the technology.

While there is excitement around Anthropic's listing, there is also some concern from investors about its future ability to generate profits in a competitive area.

Yang Wang, a principle analyst at Counterpoint Research, said the central issue was whether it could "keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations come due in the next couple of years.

However, the share sale would give investors "direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity", Wang said.

Anthropic was started by seven former OpenAI employees, led by brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei.

Dario Amodei has been outspoken about the risks posed by AI, amounting in his view to a possible threat to human existence.

The company has called for a slowdown in the development of AI, and a greater focus on safeguards while forging ahead with plans to grow quickly and boost its financing through the public markets.

OpenAI has voiced similar sentiments and delayed its plans to list on the stock market in order to address AI safety concerns.

Technology stocks have lost value in recent weeks following the US midterm elections. Democrats, who now control of both chambers of Congress, are expected to be tougher on AI regulation. Some Democrat candidates opposed the rapid build of data centres required to run AI.

But Anthropic went ahead with its market listing, despite the market volatility, because it needed to tap into additional funds, said Marta Norton, who heads strategy at investment firm Empower.

"AI is financially demanding," Norton told the BBC. "The public markets open up the financial spigot a little bit more and so the time has come."

Broader anxieties about the AI industry remain.

Competition from low-cost rival models is growing.

Expensive computer chips, necessary for the industry to operate, are in short supply.

And the US Federal Reserve is concerned about high AI-related debt being financed through "complex and opaque" structures, according to minutes from its October meeting to discuss interest rates, as well as the high concentration of AI exposure among a small number of firms.

This can sometimes happen in religious or family settings and can be very distressing for the person at the centre of it.

There have been long-running campaigns in the UK to outlaw such practices, and in its 2024 manifesto, the Labour party promised to introduce a bill banning them.

When the government introduced its draft legislation, external in June this year, Baroness Cass was quoted in the publicity for it, external.

In it, she said: "I am pleased to see that the government is bringing forward legislation which not only gives a clearer definition of what conversion practices are, compared to previous drafts, but also what they are not."

She went on to say she looked forward to the bill receiving further scrutiny before it became law.

But asked at the Draft Conversion Practices Bill committee if she supported the bill's current form, she said simply "no".

Baroness Cass said the increased "polarisation" used in the debate around gender meant people may use the new law in a way that wasn't intended.

The current wording of the bill requires the victim to suffer "serious harm to the individual's physical or mental health, or serious alarm or distress to the individual which has a substantial adverse effect on their usual day-to-day activities".

But Baroness Cass said she worried this wording left open the possibility of "vexatious" complaints that could put therapists working with young gender-distressed people at risk of prosecution.

"Therapeutic interactions can be distressing and often are because you're discussing quite sensitive issues," she told the Today programme.

"So If a young person comes away feeling upset, distressed, angry, that might be the result of a quite appropriate therapeutic intervention but still could be judged as poor professional practice."

She told the committee that professionals working at the new NHS Gender Dysphoria Clinics were concerned that even complaints processes that didn't result in a prosecution could be damaging.

"The problem is the chilling effect of professionals knowing that they may be open to complaint, and indeed prosecution," she told the Today programme.

Baroness Cass also raised concerns about the possible impact the new law could have on families.

She said that, for instance, if a parent stopped a child's money if they thought they might buy a "breast binder or hormones" that this may also fall within the scope of the bill and result in prosecution.

Asked about her apparent support for the bill when it was first published, Baroness Cass said that she was in favour of the idea but had not had the time to read the details before the press release was to be published, but went ahead and gave the quote anyway.

When she published her report on gender identity services for young people in 2024, she described conversion practices as "abhorrent". She says she still feels no LGBT people should be subjected to conversion practices.

She told the committee she wants "a bill that protects the people it's supposed to protect, but doesn't accidentally entrap those who you don't want to [entrap]".

The bill has received support from several LGBT charities, such as Stonewall, and organisations like the British Association for Counselling and Psychotherapy.

The government said: "We want to get this ban right, which is why we have put this draft bill forward for pre-legislative scrutiny.

"We welcome both Baroness Cass's support for taking action to end abusive conversion practices, and her comments on the need for legislation to avoid adverse consequences.

"We will take all evidence put forward by the committee seriously as we move forward in ending almost a decade of delay for LGBT+ people who should never have to suffer abuse in an effort to change who they are."

The committee hearings continue.

headline: How the UK's extreme heat is shifting the conversation about air-con
body:
Mandy Bourne lives with her 80-year-old mum in a top-floor social housing flat in the West Midlands. Both struggle with health conditions exacerbated by the recent heatwaves.

For Mandy, temperature shifts can trigger flare-ups of her chronic lung condition. "I've got COPD and sometimes I can't breathe," she explains.

Across the UK, solid brick homes like theirs quietly absorb heat the way they have for decades. Charged-up walls radiate warmth back into rooms that never get the chance to cool.

Mandy says she is constantly reaching for her inhaler as her flat overheats. "It's red hot in the flat. The sun is just beaming in."

Many homes are built to radiate warmth back into rooms

That retained warmth can push night-time temperatures in urban centres up to 7C higher than the surrounding countryside. This is the urban heat island effect and it is at its most dangerous in the early hours when bodies need cooler air and cannot find it. Modelling of a previous West Midlands heatwave by researchers from the University of Birmingham reached the bleak conclusion that the heat island impact alone accounted for roughly half the 130 heat-related deaths.

Jo Shields, head of sustainability for Mandy's housing association Walsall Housing Group, known as whg - which owns 23,000 homes across Walsall and the Midlands - hears the same complaint time and again. "The heat gain stays within the concrete or the brick," she says, "so the night-time cooling becomes harder".

Mandy Bourne lives with her 80-year-old mum in a top-floor social housing flat in the West Midlands. Both struggle with health conditions exacerbated by the recent heatwaves.

For Mandy, temperature shifts can trigger flare-ups of her chronic lung condition. "I've got COPD and sometimes I can't breathe," she explains.

Across the UK, solid brick homes like theirs quietly absorb heat the way they have for decades. Charged-up walls radiate warmth back into rooms that never get the chance to cool.

Mandy says she is constantly reaching for her inhaler as her flat overheats. "It's red hot in the flat. The sun is just beaming in."

Many homes are built to radiate warmth back into rooms

That retained warmth can push night-time temperatures in urban centres up to 7C higher than the surrounding countryside. This is the urban heat island effect and it is at its most dangerous in the early hours when bodies need cooler air and cannot find it. Modelling of a previous West Midlands heatwave by researchers from the University of Birmingham reached the bleak conclusion that the heat island impact alone accounted for roughly half the 130 heat-related deaths.

Jo Shields, head of sustainability for Mandy's housing association Walsall Housing Group, known as whg - which owns 23,000 homes across Walsall and the Midlands - hears the same complaint time and again. "The heat gain stays within the concrete or the brick," she says, "so the night-time cooling becomes harder".

Last summer, as the region baked, the residents of Ellum Pointe - a whg scheme for the over-55s - began telling their landlords they simply could not cool their flats. The response was improvised.

"We took the community room, closed all the windows and doors, and we put a mobile air-conditioning unit in there," Shields says. "And basically, we created an internal cool room." She likens it to the warm spaces opened during the pandemic for people who couldn't afford to heat their homes.

Shields' job has previously focused on decarbonising - reducing the emissions from the housing stock - but she now has to balance those pressures with the need to adapt homes to rising heat. Across the country, landlords are facing similar choices.

As Britain enters a new kind of summer, with homes built to trap warmth and heatwaves intensifying, two questions loom: should we embrace air conditioning despite its costs and consequences, and how much should we spend on adapting homes versus cutting carbon?

For 40 years, wealthy countries have focused heavily on cutting the carbon emissions that cause climate change, known as mitigation. Adaptation such as designing housing so it is more resilient to hotter temperatures and installing air conditioning has not always had the same focus.

Reducing emissions was seen as morally right because richer nations produced most of the gases that have warmed the planet. And with that focus came a funding imbalance.

In 2023, $1.8tn was given to mitigation, while adaptation did not secure even 5% of that – it scraped $65bn globally.

Spending too much on adaption was seen by many as giving up on the fight against climate change. But this mainstream view has now been challenged.

In a memo published last year, Bill Gates - a man who has poured billions into clean technology - argued that the climate movement's "doomsday" fixation on temperature targets had diverted money from the things that most improve lives in a warming world.

Climate change is serious, he wrote, but "will not lead to humanity's demise". Governments, he added, should be investing in cooling for the countries that need it.

The publication sparked backlash from climate scientists who accused Gates of making arguments based on "false dichotomies" - pitting mitigation and adaptation against each other.

Some, including US President Donald Trump, saw it as sign that the billionaire was "finally" supporting the belief that climate change was a hoax.

Gates insisted he was not arguing against cutting emissions, but rather for spending money where it saves the most suffering.

The row that followed exposed the real fault line that's coming to the surface this summer: not whether to cut carbon or adapt to the heat – but how much to spend on each.

There's another reason that muddies the waters and helps explain why cutting carbon became the prime focus – it was investable. Heat pumps and EVs can be sold. Spending on shade, ventilation and cooler hospitals and homes all produce little in the way of bankable returns - even if it reduces costs of climate change long term.

Baroness Brown - also known as the engineer Julia King, who chairs the adaptation committee of the government's Climate Change Committee - argues this imbalance is written into UK law.

Under the Climate Change Act, the mitigation half of her committee recommends legally binding carbon budgets that ministers must deliver and are marked on every year.

Adaptation has no such teeth: the government writes its own risk assessment and its own plans.

"Essentially, the government writes an essay, and our job is to say, is it doing the things it said would do in its essay. It's not actually to say, are these things any good."

Her committee has spent, she says, "almost 20 years pulling our hair out" - but this year has been different. With exquisite timing it produced a report just as the first heatwave was striking Britain in May - urging lawmakers to set hard adaptation targets.

"We've actually looked at the difference that providing some sort of support with cooling for the 30% of most vulnerable homes, and cooling in our hospitals, [with] preventive care visits. The modelling we've done suggests that that would reduce 40% of the increase in heat-related deaths that are predicted for 2050."

"We're saying these are the actions that can make a big difference."

One of the most controversial ideas in the report is on air conditioning. Right now, only 5% or so of English homes have a cooling unit. The Committee recommends fitting these devices in hospitals and care homes within 10 years, and schools in 25 years.

This goes against years of government advice that passive cooling was the preferred method - using shade, ventilation and other design features to bring down temperatures, not mechanical means.

Prof Mat Santamouris from the University of New South Wales, is the world's most-cited researcher on urban overheating.

Machines, he argues, should be the last line of defence: reflective roofing alone, in one of his studies, dragged indoor temperatures from around 43C towards 30C, while a ceiling fan gives comfort for a fraction of the cost.

Putting up unshaded glass towers in cities, he says, is "crazy". "We cannot air-condition our way out of climate change."

Santamouris is scathing about who is driving the air con demand - the industry, he says, is "extremely powerful" – adding that passive cooling adds its own economic growth, as money is spent on plumbers and builders.

"We cannot air-condition our way out of climate change," says Prof Santamouris

Against him stand those who think Britain's hostility to cooling has curdled into a type of masochism.

David Lawrence, of the Centre for British Progress think tank, puts it plainly: we don't tell people to insulate their homes in winter and then skip the radiators. So why insist shade and shutters are enough in summer?

He points out that air conditioning is standard now in offices, hotels and shops, "but we don't expect it for schools and hospitals - which is kind of odd, because those are places where millions of people are every day", and where heat measurably dents concentration, learning and health.

This dispute over the pros and cons of the technology is becoming political.

Some London councils, following a planning "cooling hierarchy", say low-energy ways of keeping homes cool should be prioritised over air conditioning and in a small number of cases have ordered property owners to remove them; the Conservative front bench calls it "dark ages" miserabilism; other MPs and political commentators demand an "air-con revolution".

Since April, in England and Wales the Boiler Upgrade Scheme has offered £2,500 towards a reversible air-air heat pump: a machine that warms a home in winter and cools it in summer. It is, in all but name, Britain's first air-conditioning subsidy - but it is badged as a heat pump, and only worth a third of the £7,500 for a heating-only model.

Such has been the silence around this grant, that in its first month only around 45 households claimed it. By comparison, the numbers claiming a heating-only model ran into the thousands.

In Scotland homeowners can also get a £7,500 grant for a heat pump via its Home Energy scheme - but for air-air versions that could offer cooling there is no funding at all. And in Northern Ireland there is no universal heat pump grant offered for households.

Under the terms of the England and Wales scheme, some people cannot apply at all. It is closed to social housing and new builds - which many argue shuts out the very people most exposed.

Take Woolwich, in south-east London, where a resident called Keisha says her top-floor flat reaches 43C in a heatwave.

She calls the building "inhumane"; she and around twenty neighbours in Canada Court and Clifton Lodge are taking their landlord, the housing association PA Housing, to court over homes they say are unfit to live in.

Keisha says her top-floor flat reaches 43C in a heatwave

Even the landlord half-concedes the ground: its chief executive accepts that a growing number of residents face "uncomfortably warm temperatures … due to the changing climate", in homes "designed to keep heat in rather than keep them cool".

Keisha is exactly the tenant the state's new cooling grant might have been written for. But as a social tenant, she is barred from it.

Baroness Brown's committee finds the most deprived neighbourhoods are more than seven times as likely to be badly exposed to heat.

The government had a long-running scheme for supporting upgrades to social housing - ECO - but it will close after this year over reports of "cowboy" installations. The replacement scheme, if it continues under the new government, will not start until next year.

There is a cruel physics beneath the financial unfairness.

Air conditioning doesn't destroy heat, it moves it - out of the flat and into the street, where, Santamouris says, it warms the air your neighbours breathe and drives up the demand for still more cooling, by about a third in his studies of Sydney.

The machines keeping the financially comfortable cool make everyone else's nights worse; and as wealthier households cool their rooms, the rest fall further behind. A thermal divide, opening street by street.

And it lands on the electricity grid at the worst possible moment.

The electricity demand for cooling peaks on still, hot evenings - just as the wind drops and solar fades, leaving gas to supply the extra energy. In so doing, further greenhouse gas emissions are generated, adding bit by bit to the climate change effect – the very one driving the temperatures and the demand for air conditioning.

And the same heat that drives the demand also weakens the supply: gas turbines lose output as the air warms, and in June several UK plants had to be turned down.

But such is the scale of the heat that people are voting with their wallets - demand for portable air con units is through the roof, regardless of grants and the environment.

The evidence from experts is that we should not go down this road.

Santamouris and Baroness Brown reach for the same answer: passive cooling first, machines where genuinely needed, clean power behind them, and the lesson that France learned painfully in the deadly heatwave of 2003 - the vulnerable protected rather than left to improvise.

Cooling every home by machine would strain the grid and warm the streets, hampering the effort to slow the warming that drives the demand.

In Tokyo, Santamouris says, so many air conditioners now pump their waste heat into the air that the exhaust alone generates heat that's measured at close to a thousand watts of warming on every square metre - as much energy as falls from the sky at midday. "It's another sun," he adds with emphasis, "another sun."

"It's not the same in London. But if we continue in the same way, in some years we will have the same results."

The heat of this year and last, and the prospects of it being repeated, is a future Jo Shields is upset by.

"It's our survival," she says. Most days, she tries to bury the thought of it - "because otherwise it terrifies me."

Meanwhile, Mandy says she is grateful that the new community room with its air conditioning is providing some immediate respite for her and her mum.

Based on its popular Ranger series, this beefy number parked outside the front door of Ford's Dagenham plant can carry a load of two tonnes, tow up to four tonnes and is also shouldering the hopes of the 2,000-strong workforce that still makes engines here.

Inside the factory, the three-litre diesel engines that will power this camo-painted beast drift down a production line that has seen output cut from 90,000 engines a year to about half that over the last decade.

Once mighty, the European car industry is starting to look puny and is hoping surging defence budgets as Europe re-arms can help it flex its industrial muscles once more.

Ford is part of a bid for the British Army's Light Mobility Vehicle (LMV) programme

Ford is part of a joint venture with defence specialists General Dynamics and Ricardo bidding for a Ministry of Defence (MoD) contract to supply 9,000 vehicles over the next five to seven years to replace the Army's ageing Land Rover-based fleet.

Lisa Brankin, chair of Ford UK, says it is a chance to showcase their abilities to respond quickly to defence needs: "As a manufacturer you look at every opportunity that comes at you and this is a great opportunity that we would love to take advantage of."

This is not the first time Ford has busied itself with defence work.

Ahead of World War Two, Ford's factory in Dagenham, east London, was the largest car plant in Europe.

When war broke out, civilian car assembly stopped completely, and the factory was converted entirely to military production. Between 1939 and 1945, the Dagenham plant built 360,000 vehicles for the Allied war effort.

Ford workers in Manchester manufactured 34,000 Rolls-Royce-designed Merlin engines, which powered Spitfires and Hurricane fighter planes.

Eighty years later, the UK and European car industries are hoping that the engines of war can help defend against what one supplier told the BBC was a "terminal decline".

As Europe feels compelled to commit hundreds of billions to ramp up defence spending in the face of the menace from Russia and US reluctance to be Europe's protector, car makers that are under commercial attack from Chinese rivals have taken notice.

So can the rearmament of Europe save an auto industry and a supply chain facing crisis?

Ford is far from the only car company that sees defence as a growth industry - and one that can utilise the growing overcapacity at car plants across Europe.

French car maker Renault has signed a strategic agreement with defence giant Thales to produce military drones - targeting an output of up to 1,000 units per month. The French military and Directorate General for Armament want to tap into Renault's mass-production capabilities to bypass traditional, slower defence supply chains.

Meanwhile, Volkswagen has agreed to sell an under-used factory in Osnabruck, western Germany, which will become a military manufacturing hub in a joint venture with an Israeli-based defence investor.

Jaguar Land Rover (JLR), which makes the Land Rover, is also bidding for the same contract as Ford - as the Army retires its existing Land Rover-based fleet by 2030. JLR has also established a new dedicated business unit to support its global military ambitions.

It makes sense for under-utilised auto manufacturing capacity to switch to defence, says Mike Hawes of the Society for Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) trade association.

The UK car industry and its suppliers are heavily reliant on a few big manufacturers – Nissan in Sunderland, Toyota in Derbyshire, BMW in Oxfordshire and the biggest of them all by value of output, JLR at multiple sites in the Midlands and Merseyside.

And Hawes says the supply chain is very vulnerable.

"UK automotive output has been in decline over the last eight or nine years," he says. "We're probably half of what we were 10 years ago. Now, that's obviously going to hit the supply chain because they're not making the same number of parts. So they've got capacity. They may be quite dependent on one particular manufacturer as well."

So they will welcome "the opportunity to broaden their customer base and potentially move into defence", he says.

Just two weeks ago, JLR announced it was cutting 4,000 jobs from its 30,000-strong UK workforce in order to reduce costs to stay competitive with international – particularly Chinese – rivals. Dave Roberts of the firm Evtec, which supplies cooling systems components to JLR, is worried about the implications of this.

"JLR is the critical mass in the UK automotive manufacturing space," he says. "It is the glue that holds the whole of the sector together. Because remember, when you're making volumes for JLR, they're significantly higher than any other car maker in the UK.

"If they suffer, the ripples run deeper through the supply chain."

Earlier this week, major JLR suppliers urged the government to help automotive manufacturers move into aerospace and defence, warning that large-scale car production in the UK faces long-term decline.

Executives have warned of a "visible crack" in the UK automotive supply chain

In an open letter to the prime minister, chancellor and West Midlands Mayor Richard Parker, industry leaders argued Britain's automotive supply chain was "not in decline" but "in the wrong market".

The letter was signed by executives representing businesses with more than 8,600 direct employees, alongside the Confederation of British Metalforming, which represents about 75,000 workers.

Signatories to the letter said the redundancies were "the first visible crack" in a UK automotive supply chain supporting about 183,000 manufacturing jobs.

Across Europe, the industry is facing what Sigrid de Vries, director general of the ACEA auto industry manufacturers' association called "a perfect storm". Car makers are spending billions to shift to electric vehicles and insist that government sales targets for EVs are outpacing consumer demand.

And the EVs people are buying are increasingly from the biggest new threat to the industry – China.

In the early 2000s, Western firms saw China as a land of opportunity. The country's rapidly growing middle class had plenty of money and a seemingly insatiable appetite for cars, including the most profitable upmarket models. It was a lucrative business – the Chinese market once accounted for half of Volkswagen's profits.

However, it didn't last. China wanted a home-grown car industry and lavish state funding was ploughed into making the country a leader in high-tech businesses, including electric cars.

Today, the Chinese market is overloaded with brands, both foreign and domestic, and is characterised by cut-throat competition. Chinese car makers have focused their attention on foreign markets, and have used the transition to electric vehicles as a pathway to gaining market share. The likes of BYD, Chery and Geely are moving aggressively into Europe.

For European brands, all of this could not have happened at a worse time. The loss of the steady stream of profits from China, and the emergence of Chinese rivals on their home turf, has come after they invested heavily in producing electric vehicles (EVs). But EV sales have not increased as quickly as expected. Executives admit they have struggled to match the low production costs and development speed of the Chinese insurgents.

The result is that European manufacturers are now rushing to cut costs, while wondering what to do with expensive factories capable of producing millions more cars than they are able to sell.

Volkswagen has already announced plans to cut 100,000 jobs over the next few years. Whereas once closing plants in Germany would have been unthinkable, the company has now shuttered one in Dresden and may shut down four more. That includes a site in Zwickau, where VW spent over €1bn (£857m) converting production lines to build electric vehicles - a process that was completed just four years ago.

Industry estimates indicate that western European car plants have roughly 2.5 million vehicles worth of annual spare capacity.

Little wonder that car makers are jealously eyeing soaring defence budgets across Europe.

Sigrid de Vries says car makers are well placed to help Europe rearm.

"Many of the capabilities that defence needs are needed for and also delivered by the automotive sector," she says. "So automotive manufacturers and suppliers possess industrial assets, they possess manufacturing expertise, logistics capabilities, also advanced technologies. They have vast and also very integrated supply chains that may be relevant for Europe's broader defence preparedness objective."

But it is not that simple – security protocols, political and economic rivalries within Europe plus the fact that unless you're actually at war, the volumes will not replace the mass consumer market, all of which present challenges, she says.

"These are two very different worlds," she says. Governments want to invest in their defence capabilities and that is why it's now, more than ever, interesting for manufacturers and suppliers to see what's possible, but it will not be enough to address the underutilisation of manufacturing capacity we currently see."

If defence can't plug the yawning gaps in UK and European car manufacturing production – is it time for the henhouse to rent a room to the fox?

In other words, let Chinese companies move into European production facilities?

To offset the immense fixed costs of running idle assembly lines, legacy European and UK automakers are opening their doors to Chinese rivals.

Stellantis – owners of the Vauxhall, Fiat, Peugeot and Citroen marques – has taken a 20% stake in Chinese EV maker Leapmotor and production of the Chinese brand started in Poland two years ago. (Leapmotor then moved production to Spain after Poland voted to impose steep tariffs on Chinese EVs while Spain abstained – an example of how trade politics can get complicated.)

Nissan and Chery International UK have signed a non-binding Memorandum of Understanding for the study of contract manufacturing for Nissan to manufacture Chery vehicles at its Sunderland plant.

VW CEO Oliver Blume said in April of this year that Volkswagen was considering sharing spare European factory capacity with Chinese joint-venture partners.

In one sense it could be a win-win. European factories would have extra work while Chinese manufacturers could avoid high tariffs when selling into the US and the EU by making and exporting the cars in and from those markets.

But building cars in Europe does not automatically mean creating or saving European supply chains.

Some plants may only perform final assembly while many of the components – especially batteries – may continue to come from China.

Cultural treasures are being destroyed worldwide - so why is no-one being punished?

War may be coming. Are we psychologically ready?

Why a fresh wave of North Korean soldiers may fight in Russia's war in Ukraine

Car making is still seen as central to countries' sovereign manufacturing capability – in the old days the mantra was: "What's good for General Motors is good for America." You could say the same for Volkswagen, Mercedes and BMW for Germany and JLR for the UK.

Car plants are often the major employer in their area and support local supply chains, so job losses can hit particularly hard. That's why countries go to great lengths to protect and preserve them.

Australia is a case in point. When its final locally made car left the production line in 2017, it didn't just lose a car industry, it lost an engineering mindset and key skills, says Dave Roberts of Evtec.

"Over the next decade... ripple effects crept into all manufacturing," he says. "So they lost infrastructure capability. They lost advanced manufacturing capability.

"They're vulnerable. They're not resilient in those sectors anymore."

Ford UK's Lisa Brankin acknowledges 9,000 engines over five to seven years is a far cry from the 90,000 per year the plant used to produce – but she insists every little helps.

"It is a drop in the ocean but every single opportunity is worth having, isn't it?"

A spokesperson for the Ministry of Defence says it wants UK industry to play a "central role" in delivering thousands of modern light mobility vehicles. The spokesperson adds: "We are backing British businesses and supporting our defence industrial base with 85% of our defence spending currently staying in the UK, driving reindustrialisation and making defence an engine for growth."

It's understandable why a declining European car industry wants to gatecrash the spending splurge in the defence sector. But even if they can, right now it is hard to see how they'll ever be able to wield the muscle that they once did.

headline: Man dies in M42 crash near Birmingham Airport
body:
There were long delays due to standstill traffic on Saturday afternoon

A man died in a serious crash on the M42 near Birmingham Airport, police said.

The crash, involving a van and a lorry, happened on the northbound carriageway of the motorway between junction 5a and junction six on Saturday, just after 12:30 GMT.

The van driver, a man in his 40s, died at the scene, West Midlands Police said.

The carriageway remained closed for several hours but was fully reopened to traffic earlier on Sunday morning.

Motorists caught in standstill traffic described seeing a "huge fire" after the crash, while West Midlands Police urged motorists to avoid the area.

The driver of the lorry remained at the scene and was helping officers with their investigation as inquiries remained ongoing, a spokesperson added.

No further delays were reported on the M42 on Sunday morning, National Highways confirmed

The force said the van driver's family was told what had happened and specialist officers were offering them support.

An air ambulance was sent to the scene following the crash, National Highways confirmed, while West Midlands Police and West Midlands Fire Service attended.

Overnight resurfacing work was carried out, and officers urged anyone with dashcam footage or information about the crash to contact them.

Sgt Richard Evans said: "We are working to establish exactly how the collision happened and would ask people who were driving on that stretch of the M42 at around 12:30 yesterday to check their dashcam.

headline: Further walkout planned by NI doctors as strike ends
body:
A separate 24-hour strike will begin on Monday morning as part of the same pay dispute

A 24-hour strike by resident doctors in Northern Ireland held as part of an ongoing dispute over pay has ended, but fresh action will begin on Monday.

Consultants and specialist doctors will begin a separate 24-hour strike following the weekend, as part of the same dispute.

The British Medical Association (BMA) rejected a recommended 3.5% pay rise and wants to restore the value of doctors' pay to 2008 levels.

Health Minister Robbie Butler said he had accepted the recommended rise but could not implement it without sufficient funding for his department.

The strike action that began on Friday and ended at 07:00 GMT on Saturday by resident doctors affected non-emergency services, resulting in the cancellation of many planned outpatient appointments.

Urgent surgery and most GP services continued as normal because senior doctors remained on duty.

Monday's walkout will involve consultants and specialty, associate specialist and specialist grade (SAS) doctors and will also take place over 24 hours from 07:00 GMT.

Routine hospital and elective services are expected to be cancelled during the second strike.

But emergency care will continue under Christmas Day cover - which means full emergency cover will remain in place.

The Western and South Eastern health trusts have asked patients with appointments on Monday to attend as planned, unless their trust tells them otherwise.

The Western and South Eastern health trusts have asked patients with appointments on Monday to attend as planned, unless their trust tells them otherwise.

The South Eastern Trust said the urgent care centre at Lagan Valley Hospital would be closed on Monday and that postponed appointments and procedures would be rescheduled as soon as possible.

Butler said more than 2,200 appointments were cancelled during similar strikes in June and warned the latest action would have "real consequences for patients, waiting lists and service delivery".

Scottish medic Dr Seamus Crumley said he had taken a pay cut to work in Northern Ireland

The BMA says years of below-inflation pay rises have made it harder for Northern Ireland's health service to recruit and retain doctors.

Dr Seamus Crumley, an anaesthetics registrar who works in intensive care at the Ulster Hospital, joined Friday's picket line in Belfast.

He told BBC News NI he had taken a pay cut when he moved from Scotland last year, despite securing a more senior role.

"The medical workforce here is very, very vulnerable to losing doctors to literally anywhere else in the UK, but also to the Republic of Ireland," he said.

Steven Montgomery says doctors face burnout due to pressure on them at work

Dr Steven Montgomery, who chairs the BMA's Northern Ireland Resident Doctors Committee, said his colleagues were facing burnout and emotional distress because of pressure at work.

He said the union was "not looking for this all to be paid in one lump sum" and wanted the minister to set out a plan to restore pay over time.

Dr Oisín Fearon, a resident doctor in Belfast, told BBC News NI he had considered moving to Australia, but family and local ties had kept him in Northern Ireland.

He said he had begun the process of registering to train in the Republic of Ireland and was keeping that option open.

Health Minister Robbie Butler introduced the Health and Social Care (Staffing) bill in the assembly on Monday

Butler said he had met the BMA to explain the financial pressures facing his department, external and intended to implement the recommended award as soon as possible.

He said cumulative pay rises over the previous three years averaged 30% for resident doctors, 25% for SAS doctors and 24% for consultants.

Butler said the recommended rise was higher than that for other healthcare staff and warned that going beyond 3.5% would have "significant repercussions for nurses, teachers, police officers and indeed the entire public sector workforce".

Separately, the Northern Ireland Public Service Alliance (Nipsa) released the results of a recent ballot of its health and social care members.

It said 94% of its health and social care members backed strike action, while 97% backed action short of a strike, over growing pressures on the health and social care sector.

The union said it would consider its next steps and warned that coordinated industrial action could spread across the health service in the coming weeks.

headline: How we formed a friendship to blend our families
body:

When TV personality Laura Anderson announced she was going on holiday with her ex-partner's ex-wife Natasha Gray and their children, some friends were sceptical.

"They'd say to be wary of that relationship and not see it as genuine," she says.

While there is no formal title for the mums and dads of your child's half-siblings, Laura says she thinks of Natasha as her friend.

Laura, a radio host and former Love Island contestant, has a three-year-old daughter, Bonnie, with her ex, actor Gary Lucy.

Natasha, a nurse, was with Gary for 14 years prior to Laura's relationship with him and they have four children.

Laura tells CBeebies Parenting Download how she and Natasha built a friendship to enable their children to spend time with their half-siblings.
