Also on the podcast, co-parenting expert Aaron Dale shares his experience of getting to know his son's stepfather and gives tips to other parents in a similar situation.

Laura was 14 when she found out she had a half-sister from her father's previous relationship and now the two are "very close".

She felt a responsibility to make sure her own daughter didn't "miss out on that sibling bond" and the idea of spending time with Natasha and her children developed naturally.

"Maybe there was a point that I wasn't fully ready when Bonnie was younger and I was still navigating my break-up," she says.

"But I became more comfortable with the idea and I thought, 'No, she's right. We need to make an effort'... It felt like a chance to give [Bonnie] more than just me and her."

Aaron says, when introducing new people to your children, be open and honest and allow them to ask questions

Aaron - author of The Co-Parent: A Toolkit for Parenting Together, Apart - grew up on the same estate as his half-siblings but says his father never introduced them. His two sons have different mums.

"I made a promise to myself that my sons would never feel like they were 'half' anything. My sons are brothers, full stop."

Aaron co-parents with his ex-partners and says he has a "great relationship" with the stepdad to one of his sons. He says a blended family creates "a wider circle of love" for children.

"I've seen this first hand with my son's stepfather. Not only does he have an amazing relationship with my son, but so does his daughter and their wider family."

He acknowledges it's not always straightforward but says it's the responsibility of parents to "put differences aside".

"Whatever the dynamic looks like between the adults involved, your children's relationships with their siblings deserve to be a priority."

Aaron says it's important to take time to get to know the other adults in your child's family including their values, personality, interests and what they want from life.

"Don't become so consumed with how this person might fit into your child's world that you forget to consider whether they fit into yours," he says.

He advises having a conversation about the roles you would like each other to play, what you're comfortable with and where boundaries need to be established.

You should also respect "existing bonds", he adds. "You are becoming an extension of a child's existing family, not a replacement for somebody else.

"Don't enter a child's life feeling that you have to take somebody else's place, and don't make them feel that loving you somehow means being disloyal to another parent."

Laura says her friendship with Natasha and her children means there are more people to love her daughter

Laura's advice for getting to know your blended family is to "make it about the children".

"Be as selfless as possible and remove any negative feelings you might have towards your ex," she says.

Even if you initially feel rejected when trying to establish a blended family, she urges you not to "give up at the first hurdle".

Despite scepticism from friends, Laura says she and Natasha have proven their blended family works.

"I think they definitely changed their minds once they saw pictures of us all together. They'd say, "You look so comfortable and so happy.'"

Laura says the trip she had in the summer with Natasha and their children was "one of the best holidays" she had been on.

"I felt really comfortable and it was just love all round."

Laura and Natasha have booked a staycation in the Cotswolds to celebrate Christmas with their children.

"I've got matching PJs and someone's going to come in and cook for us - and we've got a Santa coming in."

She adds: "We want to have those memories, we just want to soak it all up."

headline: ‘Environmental crimes’: Israel blamed for toxic pollution in 99% of Gaza
body:
More than three years of Israel’s genocidal war has turned Gaza into “a toxic wasteland”, with poisoned water and contaminated soil threatening the survival of Palestinians in the enclave of 2.3 million people.

Israel’s use of explosives and incendiary weapons has caused environmental contamination across more than 99 percent of Gaza, according to a new report by Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS).

“Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza includes military assaults on its environment, which are environmental war crimes threatening life now and for generations to come,” said Amitabh Behar, Oxfam’s international executive director.

“The destruction and contamination of Gaza will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival. This would breach Israel’s legal obligations under international humanitarian and human rights law,” he said in a statement.

“Palestinians living in Gaza are being exposed to toxins in multiple ways through air, food, water and via direct contact with contaminated soils and debris.”

The report shows how Israel’s destruction of buildings and the environment has contaminated the air, soil, food and water in the enclave.

It also emphasises the urgent need for a full independent investigation to identify and reduce the risks to Palestinian lives.

Pollutants from bombardment, fires, rubble and untreated sewage can reach Palestinians through the air they breathe, the water they drink and the food they eat.

The report shows how Israel’s destruction of buildings and the environment has contaminated the air, soil, food and water in the enclave.

It also emphasises the urgent need for a full independent investigation to identify and reduce the risks to Palestinian lives.

Pollutants from bombardment, fires, rubble and untreated sewage can reach Palestinians through the air they breathe, the water they drink and the food they eat.

Oxfam’s report, which uses satellite imagery, remote sensing, scientific analysis and other open-source data, gives a comprehensive picture to date of the impact of the Israeli assault on Gaza, which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians. More than 1,500 Palestinians have been killed since the so-called “ceasefire” was signed in October 2025.

In September 2025, a UN international commission of inquiry said Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. And the International Court of Justice is hearing a case of genocide against Israel. In January, the ICJ said it was plausible that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.

The report came a day after world leaders failed to reach a consensus on climate change at the 31st Climate Change Conference (COP31) of the United Nations.

Explosions, fires and the destruction of buildings and infrastructure release pollutants that settle on rubble and soil.

Wind, traffic and debris clearance send them back into the air. Oxfam’s analysis points to the highest concentrations in Gaza City, Jabalia and the North Gaza governorate.

Israel’s continuous bombardment has also generated substantial greenhouse gas emissions, with further emissions expected from clearing debris and rebuilding.

A study cited in the report estimated direct conflict emissions at more than 1.3 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) by January 2025.

By October 11, 2025, Israeli ground operations directly affected about 283sq km (109sq miles) of Gaza’s 365sq km (141sq miles), or 78 percent of the area, Oxfam estimates.

The UN Environment Programme estimates that the assault since October 7, 2023, generated 61 million tonnes of debris, which is about 29 tonnes of rubble per person living in Gaza now. More than 90 percent of Palestinians have been forcibly displaced, most of them multiple times.

Oxfam estimates that the mountains of rubble would require 2.1 million dump truckloads to clear them, equivalent to 736 trips around the circumference of the entire planet.

The amount of rubble that needs to be cleared is about eight times the 7.65 million tonnes estimated in Iraq’s Mosul during the 2017 conflict.

The report identifies at least one potential contamination source across more than 99 percent of Gaza. Gaza City, Khan Younis, Rafah, Jabalia and the Salah al-Din Street corridor showed the greatest overlap of potential hazards.

Unexploded munitions can leach contaminants into soil and groundwater as their casings corrode. Damaged vehicles, batteries and fuel stores add to the risks along military routes and former positions.

A study cited by Oxfam estimated emissions across the wider conflict cycle at 33.2 million tonnes of CO2e, including an estimate of 31.4 million tonnes of carbon emissions that will occur from reconstruction.

According to a report by Palestinian Water Authority cited by Oxfam, Gaza’s daily water supply fell from 334,107 cubic metres before October 2023 to 54,747 cubic metres in June 2024, a drop of about 84 percent. By April 2026, emergency repairs had brought it back to 130,315 cubic metres a day, still 61 percent below pre-assault levels.

Nine of 61 reservoirs were operational, with combined storage sufficient to provide 18 litres per person for one day.

Gaza’s Coastal Aquifer historically supplied 81 percent of the territory’s water. Oxfam says 97 percent of the aquifer was already chemically polluted before October 2023.

Decades of overpumping amid Israel’s air, land and sea blockade of Gaza allowed seawater to seep in. Untreated sewage, farm runoff and waste disposal added to the pollution.

In July 2026, Gaza’s Ministry of Health detected faecal coliforms in 15 of 79 groundwater wells (19 percent) tested. Oxfam identified North Gaza, Gaza City and Deir el-Balah as the areas most at risk from contaminated drinking water. An assessment in 2021 reported faecal coliforms in 2 percent of wells.

July tests found that 61 of 79 wells (77.2 percent) had total dissolved solids above 1,000 milligrams per litre, 400mg above the level at which the World Health Organization says water becomes increasingly unpleasant to drink.

By April 2024, Israel’s assault had destroyed all six of Gaza’s wastewater treatment plants. An estimated 40,000 cubic metres of raw sewage enter the Mediterranean daily, enough to fill 16 Olympic-size pools.

By April 2026, 19 percent of pumping stations and about 30 percent of the sewer network still functioned at least partly.

Gaza’s waste collection fleet fell from 261 vehicles to 48.

Both main landfills remained inaccessible. Of at least 56 temporary dumps, only 11 were accessible and operating.

These sites generally lack barriers to protect soil and groundwater. By April 2026, an estimated 1.45 million people lived in areas affected by rodents and other pests.

Before October 2023, Gaza’s farms supplied about 95 percent of the fresh vegetables people ate. By late 2025, more than 87 percent of cropland was damaged.

Oxfam says only 3 percent was accessible and undamaged.

By October 2024, the UN had reported that more than one million olive trees had been uprooted.

Oxfam identified more than 7,200 damaged greenhouses and documented the destruction of facilities that preserved and distributed Palestinian seeds.

Before the assault, Gaza’s fisheries produced about 4,660 tonnes of fish a year, with fish farms adding 750 tonnes.

In July 2026, an estimated 1.2 million people (59 percent) faced crisis levels of acute food shortages or worse, according to the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification, cited by the report.

The report also records the loss of roughly 95 percent of cattle and a collapse in fishing.

The average daily catch from October 2023 to April 2024 was 7.3 percent of its 2022 level. Oxfam warns that contaminants could enter crops and seafood as production resumes.

Gaza’s gross domestic product fell by 83 percent in 2024 to $362m, the report says.

Damage to farms, workshops and factories has stripped people of income and the means to resume work. Debris removal, repairs and farming could expose workers to asbestos, silica and other hazards for years.

Among the commerce and industry establishments assessed, 92 percent sustained damage, including 72 percent that were destroyed.

A joint World Bank, European Union and UN assessment, cited by Oxfam, put direct physical damage at $35.2bn and economic losses at $22.7bn by October 2025.

It estimated recovery and reconstruction needs at $71.4bn over a decade, including $26.3bn in the first 18 months.

Disease prevalence in Gaza recorded more than 1.9 million cases of acute respiratory infection and about 81,000 cases of acute watery diarrhoea in January and February 2026. More than 36,000 of the diarrhoea cases were among children aged below five years. Gaza recorded more than 496,000 cases of acute watery diarrhoea in 2025.

In 2024, vaccine-derived poliovirus type 2 was detected in Gaza’s wastewater. A child was later diagnosed with paralytic polio, Gaza’s first reported case in 25 years. The report also cites the detection of multidrug-resistant pseudomonas in water at primary healthcare centres.

Oxfam says the destruction of Gaza’s water, food and sanitation systems may be relevant to alleged crimes under the Rome Statute and to assessing whether Israel violated the Genocide Convention.

A genocide finding requires proof of intent to destroy a protected group, in whole or in part. Oxfam calls for full reparations where violations are established.

Its five-stage plan calls for securing access and reducing exposure, testing for contamination, screening sites and making essential repairs, treating contaminated sites and managing hazardous waste, then rebuilding with safeguards and long-term monitoring.

headline: Death toll rises after deadly Russian attacks on Ukraine
body:

Moscow has been pummelling Ukraine with nightly drone and missile barrages as the war-torn country braces for another winter while the full-scale invasion grinds through its fifth year.

An overnight strike on Dymer, about 45km (30 miles) north of the Ukrainian capital, hit a five-storey building, killing at least 11 people, Kyiv regional official Tymur Tkachenko said on Monday.

“Rescuers recovered the body of another person from beneath the rubble,” Tkachenko wrote on Telegram, confirming the death toll had risen to 11.

Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said earlier on Telegram that the dead included a teenager.

It said rescuers were searching for 11 people, including two children, who were “not responding or cannot be reached”.

Rescuers had managed to pull out survivors from the rubble, including a 79-year-old woman and a child, Tkachenko said.

Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine, reporting from Kyiv, said people were believed to still be under the rubble.

“Rescuers are still at the site, working to try to pull people out from under the rubble dead or alive,” she said.

A Russian strike on a supermarket killed three other people and wounded 15, including three children, in Vyshneve, a city just south of Kyiv, Mayor Illya Dikov wrote on Facebook.

headline: AI superintelligence ‘arriving’, warns top Meta executive
body:
Meta’s top AI executive has sounded the alarm about the risk of humanity losing control of AI, warning that superintelligence that far exceeds the human intellect is imminent.

Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang issued the warning on Sunday after an employee at AI giant Anthropic announced that he had used Claude to solve the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most difficult problems in mathematics.

Wang said the breakthrough dwarfed any human achievement for “sheer intellectual might”.

The 29-year-old executive said the milestone showed that emerging AI models will be “clearly superhuman” at improving themselves, as well as “massively accelerating” research in fields such as biology, armaments and economics.

“Superintelligence is arriving,” Wang said on X.

“How humanity acts over the next year will have great consequence on what future world we live in.”

Wang, who co-founded Scale AI before joining Meta as the tech giant’s first chief AI officer last year, said it is unlikely humankind will be able to control AI that achieves unconstrained recursive self-improvement or is “1000x smarter and more capable than humans in every field.”

“Now that we are at a point where the scientific and technical problems on capability progress are likely solved, we must not only make progress in the extremely urgent areas of safety, alignment and security, but we have to start thinking through how we progress thoughtfully,” Wang said.

“I strongly believe this is possible, but likely involves the whole industry taking meaningfully different actions from the “default path” in front of us.”

headline: Hacks, AI and conspiracy theories: why are we having so many outages?
body:
After chaos at airlines, banks and companies from Microsoft to Apple, people have become convinced the world’s systems are under attack

Nicole Reindorf’s American Airlines flight was ready for takeoff in Phoenix when the pilot came on the intercom and announced what was to become the longest nationwide aviation shutdown since 9/11.

Reindorf, 70, had seen the headlines hours before about a global Microsoft outage. She immediately suspected the two were linked in some way by AI-related threats – and that she would not get to the wedding of her best friend’s son in California.

“I presumed there had been a hack of the aviation system and that it would be down for days,” she said.

Instead, flights resumed later that day and Reindorf was able to make the wedding even if she missed that night’s rehearsal dinner. But passengers appeared to be convinced of two things, she said: “That it was a cyber-attack and that we were not going to be told the truth about it.”

This was not an isolated view. What happened in the days after the incident, which began on Thursday 12 November, left many wondering if the US, and the western world, was under a coordinated assault. By Tuesday big US banks, Apple, and the National Security Agency had also been affected by technical glitches. Researchers also flagged a cyber-attack that targeted 178 organisations worldwide, although the financial losses appeared to be small.
full:
After chaos at airlines, banks and companies from Microsoft to Apple, people have become convinced the world’s systems are under attack

Nicole Reindorf’s American Airlines flight was ready for takeoff in Phoenix when the pilot came on the intercom and announced what was to become the longest nationwide aviation shutdown since 9/11.

Instead, flights resumed later that day and Reindorf was able to make the wedding even if she missed that night’s rehearsal dinner. But passengers appeared to be convinced of two things, she said: “That it was a cyber-attack and that we were not going to be told the truth about it.”

This was not an isolated view. What happened in the days after the incident, which began on Thursday 12 November, left many wondering if the US, and the western world, was under a coordinated assault. By Tuesday big US banks, Apple, and the National Security Agency had also been affected by technical glitches. Researchers also flagged a cyber-attack that targeted 178 organisations worldwide, although the financial losses appeared to be small.

The truth is more prosaic. The chaos of the previous weeks – grounded planes, frozen email servers, iPhone outages – appears, on closer examination, to be more a string of coincidences than anything else, in part driven by fears over advancing artificial intelligence.

But the narratives that have sprung up around it are a measure of an unstable and frenetic global mood, which is dealing with two powerful trends: the rot of decades-old infrastructure from chronic underinvestment and the genesis of some of the most powerful technology humanity has made – AI.

The failure that delayed Reindorf’s takeoff originated with a faulty router in the city of El Dorado, Arkansas, population 16,609.

That router was installed in the midst of a maintenance procedure that has been under way for more than two decades. In 2002, the US government contracted a small company, now known as L3Harris, to modernise the communications system of the Federal Aviation Authority (FAA), in charge of America’s airports. As a part of it, L3Harris has been tearing up communication lines made of copper wire across the country, and replacing them with fibre optic cables.

This glacial undertaking sparked a sudden and unprecedented catastrophe – the router, newly replaced, misfired and caused air traffic communications across the US to crash, bringing all departing flights nationwide to a grinding halt. More than 18,000 flights were cancelled.

L3Harris’s contracts, which have now run into the billions of dollars, are one emblem of where the world is today: mired in ageing infrastructure that is slowly failing, yet immensely costly to replace.

There is a broad sense that governments everywhere are not equipped to deal with this. In the US, oversight reports have been urgently calling for upgrades to the FAA for years. The FAA only announced that it would phase out the use of decades-old floppy discs containing vital weather and other critical information just last year.

Meanwhile, there are more subtle issues around other incidents, such as the Microsoft outage. An upgrade in July left in place a software bug that lurked quietly for months before a string of coincidences triggered it – overwhelming the company’s servers and halting the use of most of Microsoft’s systems worldwide. The outage halted everyday procedures such as the release of detainees in American jails and access to some patients records at UK hospitals.

It was accompanied by more chaos. A software bug at JP Morgan Chase, the largest bank in the US, delayed transactions, a disruption that rippled throughout the country’s banks and their customers. An internal update at Apple caused outages of some of its iPhone apps. Routine maintenance went awry at the US Department of Defense’s National Security Agency (NSA), temporarily disrupting the internal network the agency uses to send and receive classified information.

Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and Apple might have moved far beyond copper wire and floppy discs, mostly, but they – and software companies everywhere – have been forced to run at double the pace in recent months, because of a deluge of bugs being discovered by AI. This might not be the specific reason for those upgrades; some maintenance is routine.

But AI-driven hacking has ushered in a new reality for IT professionals. The NSA told Congress that its communication outage was a result of quick fixes to systems identified as vulnerable by AI.

To recap: this spring, Anthropic and OpenAI both released powerful AI models capable of finding bugs in lines of code. They immediately spun this to the media, suggesting that all software, everywhere, is extraordinarily vulnerable to AI-driven hacking – and offering their tools to banks and spying agencies.

Some have argued that this hype is not entirely justified, suggesting that many vulnerabilities these models discover are not particularly useful to hackers. But the threat of AI-driven hacking has changed the game.

One senior cybersecurity professional told the Guardian the relentless exposure of IT flaws had left their team “exhausted”.

AI helped to uncover a bug in the PHP programming language in October. This was followed by the discovery of a vulnerability in the Java programming language on Tuesday, followed by another bug in NGINX, a web server.

“When NGINX happened I thought, ‘Oh come on – another one?’,” said the professional.

Java and PHP are both part of the essential backbone of the internet, vital infrastructure that keeps most of the world online.

“AI is accelerating vulnerability discovery so rapidly that organisations are applying patches at a volume and pace their systems were never built to absorb,” said Jamieson O’Reilly, a cybersecurity specialist.

Tech companies are constantly finding potential bugs and fixing them. Now they have to do it a lot faster, said O’Reilly: “The volume and speed of AI-driven discovery makes their problems far more acute.”

The backdrop to all this was a cybersecurity narrative already running at a fraught pitch due to the hacks of supermarket fridges across Europe, global scares such as the discovery of the flaw in PHP and the multibillion-dollar hack of the Binance cryptocurrency exchange.

Social media filled the gaps where organisations could not immediately supply information. Laura Loomer, a prominent conspiracy peddler, posted on X that “we are clearly being attacked by foreign adversaries via cyber-attacks”, adding “go get cash”. On TikTok, there are posts about a #90daypoweroutage, a conspiracy theory sparked by a nationwide test of the US emergency alert system – and a Simpsons clip.

The consequences of conspiratorial thinking can be seen at Costco, a bulk-buying retailer, where there has been a rise in emergency prep sales including purchases of generators, and general “pantry-loading” in the UK. Analysts at Mizuho Bank said this was a result of “consumer anxiety” following the outages and “apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media”.

These concerns have not been confined to the fringes. The UK government recently told its citizens to stock up on three days’ worth of cash, among other basic items, as part of a readiness-for-crisis campaign.

Stephan Lewandowsky, a professor of cognitive psychology at the University of Bristol, whose research centres on the spread of myths and misinformation, said the “clustering” of events such as multiple outages “can be perceived as being indicative of purposeful coordination rather than chance”.

Feeding into the anxiety, there have also been examples of state and criminal actors causing disruption, from Russia targeting undersea internet cables to last year’s crippling of Britain’s biggest carmaker, Jaguar Land Rover, which give credence to public concerns. A solution, said Lewandowsky, was “for responsible governments to be transparent and accurate in their communications” in order to suppress wilder explanations.

Taken together, experts say that the string of outages highlights the stunning fragility of US and global infrastructure, where a single mistake or malfunction can bring entire transportation, communication, and security systems to a standstill.

“We’ve built a world in which essential systems are so interconnected that a failure in one can just cascade through those systems really quickly,” said Aarathi Krishnan, the founder of Raksha Intelligence Futures, a global intelligence firm. “All of our systems, whether it’s comms, finance, capital, all of it, are so interconnected and concentrated, it creates a dependence. And that dependence creates fragility.”

What can be done? It is unclear. AI-driven bug discovery is not going to slow down and the legacy systems the world is grappling with are what they are. Infrastructure is the often overlooked backbone of society and those who decades ago built networks of road and air traffic systems and electrical grids could not have anticipated these modern threats.

Mike Chapple, the faculty director of Notre Dame University’s business computer science programme, said it was “unfortunate” that one faulty router could have such an effect on a nation’s aviation communication system.

“That just points to a design that isn’t resilient – it shouldn’t be designed in a way that one failure at one location can cause the whole nationwide system to come tumbling down.”

More troubling hacks, and more conspiracy theories, are probably on the horizon. The senior cybersecurity professional said heightened public awareness of cyber disruption had led to hypersensitivity about any incident.

“It’s like the tide has gone out on cybersecurity in terms of public perception, and there’s the same amount of wrecks out there as there have been for years. Any time you change a complex system, stuff happens.”

However, the professional is concerned that AI, with its capacity to identify flaws, help plan attacks and execute them, will be harnessed by “already very competent” adversaries. Referring to the general state of IT security around the world, the source added: “Thank goodness we haven’t had an AI-sourced vulnerability that is easy to exploit. Because that would be carnage.”

For many, though, recent events have been bad enough.

When Josephine’s* prescription request for lithium for her bipolar disorder was lost “in the ether” during the global Microsoft outage, she admits she was “freaking out”.

“My medication is life-changing and keeps me stable,” said the 26-year-old, a student living in the east of England. After an agonising wait, she was finally able to collect her prescription, but the experience has left her deeply troubled.

“For myself and many others, we struggled to access life-saving medication,” she said. “It is alarming there was no contingency plan.”

* Name has been changed

Additional reporting by Jane Clinton

headline: Princess of Wales speaks about impact of cancer diagnosis in BBC film Heal
body:
Documentary records Catherine taking on Three Peaks challenge and finding ‘sense of hope alongside uncertainty’

The Princess of Wales has spoken candidly about the impact of her cancer diagnosis in a BBC documentary to be aired later this month.

“Cancer does change you,” Catherine, 44, says in the trailer for the 30-minute programme. “It changes your body. It changes you physically, but there’s a much, much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you.”

The film records Catherine taking on the Three Peaks challenge – climbing the three highest mountains in England, Scotland and Wales in 24 hours – and meeting with other people undergoing cancer treatment. Described by the BBC as a “highly personal film”, the documentary, titled Heal, will be shown on BBC One on 29 November.

The trailer emerged as it was reported that King Charles will voluntarily pay “mansion tax” on relevant royal household properties, despite crown exemption. The high-value council tax surcharge, often referred to as a mansion tax, will take effect in 2028 and apply to properties valued at more than £2m.

Catherine was diagnosed with an undisclosed form of cancer in early 2024, for which she received chemotherapy, and by January 2025 announced she was in remission.

She was treated at the Royal Marsden hospital in London, a world-leading oncology centre, with funds from the distribution of the documentary, which will also be broadcast in other countries, going to the Royal Marsden cancer charity.

headline: Natural England could be abolished as part of quango cull, says Louise Haigh

UK central bank will want to avoid echoes of expensive US Federal Reserve revamp that led to Trump clash

Andrew Bailey may spend his days closely watching developments in the strait of Hormuz or US stock markets for signs of shocks to the global economy – but the Bank of England’s governor has a £160m problem brewing much closer to home.

A secretive major revamp of the Bank’s historic headquarters in the heart of London’s Square Mile presents a huge test of Bailey’s project management skills. The central bank, with its reputation staked on carefully counting the nation’s pennies, will be keen to avoid delays, budget-busting or any echoes of the expensive US Federal Reserve revamp that left his former peer Jerome Powell awkwardly clashing with Donald Trump on camera.

Bailey and his senior managers believe they can modernise the Bank’s Grade I-listed structure and interiors while 3,500 staff are still busy at work on site.

By the summer of 2028, 1,400 Bank staff who work in a nearby office at 20 Moorgate will be relocated to Threadneedle Street, have taken voluntary redundancy or have been offered an alternative job in a new outpost in Leeds, also being refurbished.

It appears a unique project for Britain’s struggling building trade: overhaul a site with a globally recognised exterior; preserve its Roman mosaic floors, stone columns and vaulted, ornate ceilings while keeping exact floorplans under wraps, for fear of terror attacks.

The Bank itself began in rented premises in 1694, moving to Threadneedle Street in 1734. Nicknamed the Old Lady of Threadneedle Street after a satirical cartoon of William Pitt the Younger, it has been refashioned and remodelled – first by Sir John Soane between 1788 and 1833 and then again in the 1920s when the interior was largely demolished and rebuilt.

The building is owned by the Bank, which was given independence to set interest rates by Gordon Brown in 1997, and, after the 2008 financial crash, it was later handed responsibility for regulating the banking sector by George Osborne.

Cash to fund the scheme will come from an estimated £100m of savings each year for three years that the Bank says will accrue from 450 redundancies and other cost savings. As one member of Bank staff told the Guardian: “It’s like there is a leaving party every week.”

What the Bank wants to avoid is a repeat of the delays and cost overruns that dogged the Federal Reserve in Washington, which led to Trump threatening the US central bank with court action.

Over the life of the Fed’s renovation project, construction costs have soared. The initial budget of $921m (£696m) in February 2020 was revised several times before December 2024, when it hit $2bn. Construction was supposed to be completed in mid-2024 but is now expected to run until December 2027. The final cost is likely to be nearer $2.5bn.

The Bank’s scheme is on a much smaller scale, and pales against the possible £60bn it will cost to renovate the Palace of Westminster. It is more akin to the £80m Elizabeth Tower restoration.

What Bailey will want to avoid is joining the Elizabeth Tower, which houses Big Ben, as the subject of parliamentary scrutiny after its budget doubled and then rose by a further 20%, giving ammunition to critics who have long accused the Bank of mishandling its core purpose of helping to manage the economy by setting interest rates at the appropriate level.

The Bank project was first announced in July 2025 and work was due to start this month, but it was only in October, with a month to spare, that the construction company Sir Robert McAlpine was awarded the building contract.

Described as an “incredibly complex project”, it aims to transform the neoclassical building, which sits opposite the Royal Exchange and adjacent to the Mansion House, into what some staff hope is a Google-like workplace of friendly office spaces, breakout rooms and in-house cafes.

The Bank says there will be no delays, citing the appointment of architects last November. A project manager, a cost consultant and a firm of engineers were also signed up, and they have already begun evaluating budgets and timescales.

A Bank of England spokesperson said: “As part of our plans to preserve our historic Threadneedle Street office we are considering how best to renovate the site and optimise our running costs. All our procurement processes aim to deliver value for money.”

after newsletter promotion

Bailey’s team – based in a grand part of the Bank known as the Parlours – will need to judge the cost implications of meeting new regulations on fire safety, accessibility, electrical testing – with the fire at Notre Dame mid-renovation still fresh in the memory – new plumbing and the need to have a more environmentally friendly building with heating based on renewable sources.

And that’s not to mention the security of the building while all this goes on. Bailey will be concerned that the 400,000 bars of gold, worth more than £200bn, and £100m of bank notes in the vaults are safe from terrorists and thieves.

A further complication is the fate of the Bank’s museum, which is now open to the public and tucked away in the side of the building, facing on to Bartholomew Lane.

Some senior staff had wanted to relocate the museum into the central quad and have the 100,000 visitors a year – mainly schoolchildren – march through the main entrance. Others wanted to have cafe space near the entrance to make the Bank appear more modern and appealing to visitors.

Vivienne Grafton, the executive director of central operations, told the Architects Journal: “This is an opportunity to breathe new life into a legacy building, not through radical reinvention, but through thoughtful, intelligent transformation.”

But architectural plans have yet to be agreed with the local authority – the City of London Corporation – and Historic England, which must sanction the proposed work on a building considered a cornerstone of Britain’s financial district.

Anna Joynt, a senior architect and heritage expert at the London practice of Allies and Morrison, said it was common for large, complex historic building projects to begin preparatory works before full consent has been given.

“There may be bones of the future scheme in place but the wider scheme may not be developed enough to submit for listed building consent – which needs a lot of detail,” she said.

“It’s fairly common to split out simpler early enabling works and get permission for them in advance of a main scheme. It means work can start earlier and save money as the longer you wait the more things cost.”

There has been some tangible progress on the scheme. The roof of the main portico is clad in scaffolding to allow for repairs. And last year the Bank secured planning permission to overhaul one small section – an area known as the former governor’s secretaries’s offices, which will have their plasterboard walls taken out and the space opened up and modernised.

As for the rest of the 1.4-hectare (3.5-acre) site, staff must wait and see.

headline: Meet Phil, the bar-tailed godwit tracked on a 6,800-mile round trip to Siberia
body:
Scientists use lightweight tracker to map wading bird’s extraordinary migration from Norfolk to the Arctic and back

A bar-tailed godwit called Phil has completed a 6,800-mile journey from Norfolk to Siberia and back again, in the first UK mapping of the endurance feats of this long-distance migrant.

A wading bird not much larger than a pigeon, the bar-tailed godwit is known for making the longest recorded non-stop migratory flight of any bird. Populations that visit Britain spend summers breeding in the Arctic Circle before retreating to the unfrozen wetlands of Britain in winter. In 2022, one bar-tailed godwit made the longest recorded non-stop flight, 13,560km over 11 days from Alaska to Tasmania.

The full extent of Phil’s long-distance capabilities has been revealed thanks to RSPB scientists using a tracker weighing just 6g. This was fitted to Phil in January by the Wash Wader Research Group, which named the bird in honour of Phil Ireland, the group’s leader for many years.

Since then, the tracker has followed Phil on his journey from the Wash to the Wadden Sea coasts of the Netherlands, Denmark and Germany in March, and then on to the Taymyr peninsula in central Siberia in late May. On his successful return journey, Phil cruised over the Arctic Ocean off northern Norway, pausing on three small Norwegian islands before returning to the Wadden Sea.

On his successful return journey, Phil cruised over the Arctic Ocean off northern Norway, pausing on three small Norwegian islands before returning to the Wadden Sea.

He has now been recorded safely back at RSPB Snettisham on the edge of the Wash, where thousands of birds flock together at the highest of tides in one of the greatest wildlife spectacles of a British winter.

“It’s amazing to think that a bird we tagged here on the Wash in January has travelled thousands of miles to Siberia and made it all the way back again,” said Jeff Kew, a coastal adviser for the RSPB.

“By tracking Phil, we’re reminded why protecting migratory birds needs to be a global effort. Many species cross borders and depend on a whole network of wetlands along the way.”

Bar-tailed godwits that visit Britain use part of what is known as the east Atlantic flyway, a migratory superhighway that stretches from the Arctic to South Africa and is a route for millions of birds each year. The vast mudflats of the Wash are a vital feeding and resting place for scores of species.

Dr Nigel Clark, of the Wash Wader Research Group, said: “The Wash is the UK’s single most important coastal wetland for migratory waders and spectacular numbers can be seen here in autumn and winter.

“But tracking birds like Phil the godwit shows us how connected the Wash is with the rest of the flyway. This network of sites is more important than any single ‘service station’ alone.”

headline: Grand Theft Auto fans skip work and pull all-nighters to play new instalment
body:
Hotly anticipated Bonnie and Clyde-inspired adventure GTA VI has gamers glued to their screens around the world

Grand Theft Auto fans around the world pulled all-nighters, skipped work and school, and attended overnight launch parties to vicariously embark on police chases and coordinate robberies as the latest instalment of the eagerly anticipated series arrived.

GTA VI, a Bonnie and Clyde-inspired crime adventure game set in the fictional US state of Leonida, was launched at midnight on Wednesday after a 13-year wait.

The hype around the release led to schools encouraging pupils not to miss lessons in anticipation of “GTA flu”, a term coined for the swathe of absences when GTA V was released in 2013, which is expected to recur over the coming weeks. The human resources platform Remote said there had been a 32% increase in leave requests worldwide on Thursday.

Birchgrove comprehensive school in Swansea, south Wales, had warned parents and carers that despite the “considerable excitement”, studies should remain a priority.

The Sandon secondary school in Essex entered students into a raffle for £10 Amazon vouchers, a lunchtime queue-jump pass and free Christmas dinners as incentives to stop them bunking off to play as the game’s dual protagonists, Jason and Lucia.

Narendra Modi, India’s prime minister, took a different approach in a country with an estimated 550 million gamers. Modi posted 10 images on X modelled ‌on the game’s artwork that compared India today with the time of GTA V’s release.

Narendra Modi, India’s prime minister, took a different approach in a country with an estimated 550 million gamers. Modi posted 10 images on X modelled ‌on the game’s artwork that compared India today with the time of GTA V’s release.

The Indian politician, who has stepped up efforts to appeal to younger voters since youth-led protests over jobs and education, wrote: “India is playing a whole new game!”

Downing Street said Andy Burnham would not be playing the new instalment. Asked whether the UK prime minister would be exploring Vice City, the Grand Theft Auto maker Rockstar’s fictional take on Miami, a spokesperson said: “His diary is very full.”

The launch of GTA VI generated more than 2.6m posts on social media in 24 hours, according to social media monitor Visibrain.

Approximately 1,850 messages about the game were published per minute – 7% more than the number of posts at the start of the 2026 men’s Fifa World Cup.

Among the game’s fans is Sean Little, a self-employed painter and decorator. He persuaded his wife and daughter to sign a “non-interference contract”, giving him a week off dad duties to play in peace in Dumfries and Galloway, Scotland.

Myles_Away, a UK-based streamer on the Twitch platform, told the BBC he planned to play for “13 or 14 hours” on Thursday.

after newsletter promotion

He said: “I played all last night, and then I slept, woke up, and [came] right into this interview,” adding: “Obviously not everybody is able to drop the money required. [Consoles] are very expensive at the moment, so they are able to experience the story through streamers.”

Jacob Joel, a 30-year-old IT professional in Bengaluru, southern India, took the day off to play in a gaming cafe. “We waited around 13 long years to get into GTA VI,” he said. “That is a nostalgic feeling.”

In Bangkok, British tourists Kyle McKee and Emily Todd reserved a PS5 console, TV and a sofa at a gaming centre. McKee, 27, told the AFP news agency: “It’s the fear of missing out, honestly.”

The launch also surpassed broadband records in the UK. Virgin Media O2 said its evening traffic between 8pm and 10pm on Wednesday was 9.4% higher than the previous record, set last week by “pre-loading” for GTA VI.

BT and EE networks also recorded their highest-ever home broadband traffic peak in the lead-up to the release.

Data from the two brands found that Fort Augustus, in Loch Ness, Scotland, recorded the biggest percentage uplift in gaming download traffic anywhere in the UK since the start of the pre-downloads last week.

Sony’s shares were up 2.92% on the Tokyo stock exchange after the global launch, with the analytics firm Omdia estimating that GTA VI could generate $3.2bn (£2.4bn) in sales by the end of the year.

headline: Don’t blame cyber-attacks for recent outages. The real villain is the US economy | Bruce Schneier
body:
Our tech infrastructure is riddled with problems. But they’re all downstream of the incentives baked into shareholder capitalism

It’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft, the FAA, a handful of banks, United Airlines, an unnamed classified NSA network, and Apple. People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyber-attack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none.

The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyber-attack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.

None of them should surprise, though. Our computerized infrastructure is both vulnerable and fragile.

Much of it is old and has been incrementally patched and upgraded over the decades. A surprising amount of it is maintained by hobbyists, without any recompense. There often aren’t good backup systems. And more and more of it is centralized, meaning that individual failures have cascading consequences across many different aspects of our lives and society.

A lot of our tech infrastructure just barely works. And when it fails, it can fail badly. It’s the very opposite of resilience.

The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyber-attack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.

None of them should surprise, though. Our computerized infrastructure is both vulnerable and fragile.

Much of it is old and has been incrementally patched and upgraded over the decades. A surprising amount of it is maintained by hobbyists, without any recompense. There often aren’t good backup systems. And more and more of it is centralized, meaning that individual failures have cascading consequences across many different aspects of our lives and society.

A lot of our tech infrastructure just barely works. And when it fails, it can fail badly. It’s the very opposite of resilience.

There are a lot of technological reasons why this is true, but they are all downstream from the economic ones. The technologies we rely on are built and maintained within our economic system – and that’s where the core problems lie.

Security, safety, resilience, redundancy and recoverability are all essential parts of reliable technology, but they are all costs. More importantly, they are costs that don’t generate near-term profits.

Modern shareholder capitalism, and private equity in particular, prioritizes near-term profits over everything else. This squeezes all apparent inefficiencies – and, additionally, all other positive intangibles – out of a company in pursuit of those profits.

Market competition, essential for the forces that nudge companies to provide better services, is another perceived inefficiency. Monopolization removes it in pursuit of near-term profits.

From the perspective of a quarterly budget, spending on reliability measures is an inefficiency. They’re expenses that don’t generate revenue. They feel wasteful … until something bad happens.

But, if you’re lucky, you can push the costs of failure on to society, further increasing profits. So, we get stranded in airports when planes don’t fly, or have to deal with the fallout when we can’t withdraw money from our bank accounts.

The effects of those economic pressures are brittle systems, with single points of failure and cascading failure modes. They’re more susceptible to cyber-attack – both human and AI-fueled – and more susceptible to random mistakes.

The more we allow unregulated capitalism to privatize gains while socializing risks, the more we should expect these sorts of failures.

Upgrading our computerized systems, increasing their reliability, removing single points of failure, and making them more resilient are all technical problems. But they won’t happen until we fix the political and economic ones.

We need to change the economic incentives that make it profitable to operate these systems just at the edge of functionality, and to push the costs of failure on to all of us. Fixing that requires regulation – with enforcement and meaningful fines – and stringent antitrust enforcement.

But while that’s all easy to say, it’s much harder to implement – especially in the US where monied interests have such a tight hold on the legislative agenda. Until this changes, we should expect lots more of these sorts of failures in the future.

Bruce Schneier is a security technologist who teaches at the Harvard Kennedy School at Harvard University and the University of Toronto’s Munk School

headline: ‘The doom of humanity’: will the quest to make robotic hands render us obsolete?
body:

Just outside Luton, in an Amazon warehouse the size of four football pitches, yellow shelving units pirouette in a digitally choreographed dance. Tubs containing a Lego Spider-Man kit, followed by dishwasher tablets, followed by a pouch of muscle building protein powder whiz along conveyor belts, until they arrive at a human being tasked with stacking the shelving unit that has come to a stop in front of their workstation. This, Amazon says, is the “symphony of people and technology” to which the retail giant owes its success.

Following a barrage of negative publicity about working practices, Amazon began to open up its fulfilment centres to carefully controlled free public tours a decade ago. Our guide tells us about the competitive rates of pay Amazon workers receive, their pensions, dental cover and options for flexible working. Her delivery is somewhat robotic.

“You will see robots and humans working in harmony,” she declares as we move between different stations of the warehouse. Everything is designed to maximise what humans are good at, she continues, and what robots are good at – “working without getting tired”.

The one thing stopping AI taking over the world – or at least everyone’s jobs? Dexterity. Human hands are anatomical marvels that engineers have struggled for years to replicate. Experts are racing to change that

Just outside Luton, in an Amazon warehouse the size of four football pitches, yellow shelving units pirouette in a digitally choreographed dance. Tubs containing a Lego Spider-Man kit, followed by dishwasher tablets, followed by a pouch of muscle building protein powder whiz along conveyor belts, until they arrive at a human being tasked with stacking the shelving unit that has come to a stop in front of their workstation. This, Amazon says, is the “symphony of people and technology” to which the retail giant owes its success.

Following a barrage of negative publicity about working practices, Amazon began to open up its fulfilment centres to carefully controlled free public tours a decade ago. Our guide tells us about the competitive rates of pay Amazon workers receive, their pensions, dental cover and options for flexible working. Her delivery is somewhat robotic.

“You will see robots and humans working in harmony,” she declares as we move between different stations of the warehouse. Everything is designed to maximise what humans are good at, she continues, and what robots are good at – “working without getting tired”.

Almost every judgment call here seems to be made by a computer – not just where to stow items when they arrive at the warehouse (the system shines a light on to the spot on the specific shelf where the worker should place each item) but also which size box to pack something in once it’s been ordered, and even precisely how much tape to use to seal that box. The human beings are here to provide the hands, not the brains.

So far, at least, there is no hardware or software to rival a human hand. Humanoid robots – often called “embodied AI” – have made great strides over the past decade (literally, as evidenced in China’s recent five-day robot Olympics). But producing a robot that can pack a shelf, tighten a bolt and also pick a raspberry – actions that would make them useful rather than simply entertaining, actions most of us perform without any conscious effort – has proved surprisingly difficult. Replicating the breadth of function of the human hand is one of the biggest remaining challenges in robotics. Until robots are dexterous, human workers will always be necessary.

But investors are now gambling on humanoid robots soon becoming as much a part of everyday life as AI-powered large language models are for many of us today. The Chinese government has pledged to invest more than £100bn in robotics and high-tech industries over the next two decades. Earlier this year, Tesla halted production of its Model X and Model S cars so that factories could focus instead on producing Optimus humanoid robots. “Human hands have evolved to be this incredibly sophisticated machine. Your hand is actually a remarkable thing,” Tesla chief executive Elon Musk told a conference last year. “In order to create a robot that can be a generalised humanoid, you must solve the hands problem.”

Amazon employs more than 1.5 million people worldwide today. But from what I can see on the warehouse floor, it seems that if a task could be done more efficiently by a machine, Amazon would rather leave it to a robot. What will happen to these workers when the “hands problem” is solved?

And what will happen to the rest of us? Artificial dexterity combined with artificial intelligence will be hugely consequential for humanity. Forget retraining as a plumber in the age of AI – if engineers manage to replicate human hands, then potentially no job will be future-proof.

Dexterous robots that can rival a human hand are not here yet, but they are coming. What makes hands so difficult to reproduce in hardware and software? How close are robotics engineers to getting it right? And what will happen to the world of work when they do?

“The hand is our conduit between the brain and the world,” says Alistair Hunter, a hand and wrist surgeon at University College London hospitals. “The hand is our way of turning thought into action.” Hunter has spent most of his professional life seeking to understand how hands work, and how to return them to normal function when they don’t. “Hands are special because they are very complicated anatomically,” he tells me over coffee in north London. “There are 27 bones in the hand; there are nerves and muscles that control it. But behind all that is the brain, which is interacting millisecond by millisecond to understand what the hand is sensing, adjusting to that, and then providing action.”

We might assume that we owe our evolutionary advantage to our intelligence, but Hunter argues it’s actually the combination of our cognitive power and our dexterity that has given us the edge. Over the millions of years that the frontal cortex of our brains was developing, the hand evolved to differentiate itself from limbs, allowing for the development of fingers that could grasp branches and climb trees. Thumbs came next. All the great apes might have them, but ours are larger. “The joint at the bottom of the thumb – the trapeziometacarpal joint – is one of the main advances in evolution to allow us to do very fine pincer grip, very fine dexterous control between thumb, index and middle finger, but also incredible power, incredible grasp. That allowed us to manipulate things like stones and rocks, so three million years ago we started to develop tools.”

The brain is constantly coordinating the interaction between larger muscles in the forearm, which allow for power and strong grip, and smaller muscles in the hand itself that give us fine control. It also receives huge amounts of data from the hand. “The density of nerve fibres and sensory endings in the hand is enormous,” Hunter continues. As well as the nerve endings, the hand has specialist receptors that can tell our brains about very fine details: different corpuscle cells to detect vibration, roughness and smoothness, or how our fingers and hands stretch and conform around objects. “It’s that interplay between the sensory side, the motor side and the brain that makes the hand wonderful – and so difficult to replicate.”

When you pick a raspberry, your fingers sense how soft it is, whether it’s slippery, how the skin in your fingertips conforms around it. Your brain compares this information against what it expected to experience, and then recalibrates accordingly, slowing down the compression force if it feels as if the raspberry is being crushed. “That feedback loop takes about a tenth of a second,” Hunter tells me. “We’re also able to predict what that raspberry feels like – that’s called feed forward. Even before I’ve grasped it, my fingers and my hand know what pressure to put on it to pick it and not to squash it. That’s partly why you see a baby making a mess before they’ve learned that feed forward mechanism. Their hand is clumsy because it hasn’t got that predictive model.”

From striking a match to throwing a spear to playing piano, the range of tasks hands can perform is enormous. We can use them to catch, or cup them to turn them into a drinking receptacle. And they allow us to communicate – with gestures, with pens, with our thumbs over pocket-sized screens. Our hands are constantly adapting to our ever-changing needs.

It’s this breadth of function combined with adaptability that Hunter says would be such a challenge for any engineer seeking to replicate human dexterity in a robotic hand: being able to feedback and feed forward at the same time, using a model learned from years of experience and interaction with the world. That’s why robot engineers previously focused on creating task-based robots, able to perform a specific function, he adds, rather than trying to emulate everything a human hand can do.

“I think at some point they’ll be able to do it. We’ve got many, many years ahead of us, and you can see that already robots are able to walk and run. But building a computer that is able to predict the outside world and also deliver the right amount of sensory information back – that’s going to be difficult.”

If there ever was a symbol of dystopian tech, it is the robotic hand left clutching at Sarah Connor’s throat in the final scenes of the original Terminator movie. That’s the first thing I think of when I walk into the HQ of Shadow Robot, Europe’s premier manufacturer of dexterous hands, and see one of its prototypes – skeletal and grasping – mounted on a high shelf a few metres from the entrance. Then one of the office dogs bounds up to me, and I remember that I am in a cheery workspace a minute away from London’s Hampstead Heath.

Shadow Robot began in the 1980s as a collective of hobbyists and robot enthusiasts who met up in a north London attic to tinker around with scavenged materials, hoping to one day build a full humanoid. The company was founded after they received their first commercial order – for a leg – in 1997. For the last decade or so, their exclusive focus has been on hands.

In the demo room, the Shadow Dexterous Hands they have set up for me to see look almost friendly. Mounted on two outstretched motorised arms, their palms are open with their fingers curled slightly inwards, as if waiting to give me a hug, but we begin by shaking hands instead. Its right hand moves slowly towards mine, the fingers splayed, the wrist cocked in anticipation. Its grip is gentle – natural, even – but I don’t want to shake it too hard for fear of crushing it: it’s made of MDF and nylon, with textured magnetic sensors on its fingertips, and it feels very delicate. The starting price – without any kind of software or operating system – is £20,000 per hand; the full system costs £100,000. But my instinct to be gentle is mostly because it seems so human: it moves in an expressive way, as if it were animated by some sort of soul.

And it kind of is. It’s being operated by Liem Tran, robotics deployment and support manager at Shadow Robot, who is wearing gloves with sensors that track his movements, which the robot hands copy in real time. This teleoperation is a way of training the robot, showing the hands what to do, giving them a reference point on what constitutes a successful motion for any given task. Through machine learning, the hand will ultimately be able to replicate that movement without human help. The Shadow Robot company builds the hardware and basic systems; their customers – in industry, manufacturing and academic research – typically develop their own software to get what they want from the hands.

It’s a great time to be a hand roboticist, Tran says. “We don’t have anything that’s industry standardised, or anything that’s fully developed and ready for use. It’s exciting, because we’re essentially dictating what happens next with the tech. I like the idea of replicating a human in machine form and seeing where it takes us … Do you want a grape?”

The left robot hand reaches down to a brown paper bag on the table in front of us and pulls out a bunch of white grapes, holding the stalk with a delicate pincer movement between thumb and index finger. The right hand deftly plucks a lone grape and drops it into my palm. Each hand weighs roughly 4.5kg, Tran tells me, but the grape is resolutely unsquashed. I eat it. It passes me another.

This is only the first of several party tricks Shadow’s robot hands have up their sleeves. Tran shows me how they can stack plastic cups in a pyramid, gently positioning each one. They can hold a small wooden cube in one hand and build a tower seven blocks high on top of it with the other, keeping everything perfectly balanced. They can sort shapes, placing stars, cylinders and triangles into their appropriate slots in a bright plastic kids’ toy.

In one respect, it’s totally remarkable, but in another, completely mundane: these are hands, doing what hands do. And they are also doing it at the level of a small child. When Tran successfully manages to get the robot hands to put one of the shapes into the shape sorter, I find myself declaring, “Well done!” as if I were encouraging a toddler.

While these Shadow Dexterous Hands might look lifelike, they can’t generate anything like the amount of sensory data that the human hand can produce, and their learning model depends on a human showing them what to do. But Shadow has another model that’s got everyone here very excited – and it doesn’t look much like a human hand at all.

The DEX-EE hand, created for Google DeepMind and first unveiled in 2024, has only three digits and no wrist; the digits function like thumbs, making the DEX-EE look like a claw, with optical sensors on each fingertip. Much bulkier than the Dexterous Hands, it can’t handle very fine objects, but you can smack the DEX-EE with a baseball bat. Tran invites me to give it a try. I whack it a few times, but I don’t put my back into it: this model costs £60,000 per hand.

“It can take a beating,” Tran assures me. “That’s its whole purpose: it can go through hours and hours of collisions with the work surface.” The DEX-EE was designed to withstand hours of machine learning, making repeated mistakes that it can learn from. “It’s the same way that a baby learns to use their hands and fingers.” After experimentation with DEX-EE, DeepMind has been able to develop robots that can tie shoelaces, put a shirt on a hanger, and perform repairs on other robots.

Even though some of the most powerful tech companies in the world are working with hands that can learn on their own, manual labour looks to me as if it’s going to be safe, for now: these hands seem years away from being smart enough, robust enough or dexterous enough to deal with the variability workers in a fulfilment centre encounter every day.

after newsletter promotion

But Tran quietly disagrees. “Around the world, so many companies are now making all these dexterous hands. There’s a huge race for the smoothest and most human-like. They’re getting quite impressive. The price point is becoming a lot more attractive: some hands in China are less than £2,000, which is very cheap; you don’t have to worry about repair, just buy another hand,” he says. “I don’t think we’re too far off.”

Shadow Robot never set out to compete in the high-stakes fight for global domination of the hands market. When they were a collection of amateur enthusiasts, their original aim was to build a useful humanoid, a kind of robot butler. “We built this biped – it’s now in the Science Museum, which is kind of nice,” Rich Walker, director at Shadow, tells me. Then Honda unveiled its P1 humanoid. Shadow’s biped could stand and right itself if it was shoved, but the P1 could actually walk. “As far as we can tell, Honda had spent in the order of $100m on the programme of development that led to them having a biped,” Walker continues. “We were kind of put back by that.” They decided to change tack. “We thought, what would we need a robot to do or to have in order to be useful? They’d need to be able to pick things up and interact with the same objects that I can interact with. So we decided to try building some hands.”

Walker was on the dole when he first started collaborating with the Shadow hobbyists in the 1980s. With bright blue eyes behind his varifocals and a wispy grey half ponytail that struggles to contain several thick dreadlocks, he looks part wizard, part cyberpunk, and nothing like an entrepreneur. “We never set up this organisation to make money out of building robots. It was much more, ‘Let’s build robots! How do we do that?’” he says, throwing his hands up in the air again. “Making some money on the way turns out to be a good way to make sure that you can build the robots.”

When they began developing their first prototypes, Walker tells me, their aim was to build a lifelike hand, but they soon realised what a massive task that would be. They pored over anatomy textbooks, envious of the natural hardware in the human body. “If we had those materials, it would be great,” he grins. “Self-lubricating joints. Skin that regrows. We don’t have those, so we have to use other mechanisms and solutions.”

Over the years it became clear that the most commercial proposition would be for the company to focus on hands that could fulfil specific tasks. They began to move away from the hobbyist drive to build the best thing possible, and towards a business imperative to build something that companies might want to buy in large quantities. “We’re working with a wide range of people, everything from applications in nuclear decommissioning through to medical technology and care robotics and production line stuff. A really wide range of areas where people have said, ‘Could we use a robot here?’ or, ‘Could we improve our robots with things like human hands?’”

I ask Walker what he wants his robots to be used for, and he pauses for several seconds. “We want to build robots for good. At the moment, we’re looking at robots that can do tedious things that get in the way of doing something else.” He gives the example of cleaning up the workbench of a highly skilled engineer. There are clients – and specific jobs – the company has turned down, he adds. They won’t work for arms manufacturers. After some discussion, the team decided not to lend their expertise to a project that would debone carcasses, and another that involved filling sausage casings with meat. “It’s just the ick factor sometimes.” (Walker is vegan).

But when the Shadow Robot company says no, there are now many competitors that customers can go to instead. “Ten years ago, there were four or maybe five companies making robot hands, and you knew all of them, and you knew everything about all of them. And now it’s just …” Walker throws his hands up again. “I had a Chinese analyst firm contact me a year and a half ago, and they were like, ‘We have 110 robot hands on our list.’”

It’s not just China. San Diego-based Psyonic specialises in making prosthetic hands for amputees, but has branched out into robot hands, billing its products as the “future of automation” with “human-level stability”. Sharpa, based in Singapore, boasts that its model has “human-like dexterity” and can handle complex tasks such as “screwing, clipping [and] fastening”. Boston Dynamics’ Atlas humanoid is not yet on the market, but it can use nail guns and drills (deftly changing a fine drill bit in a demonstration video). Yet most of the momentum seems to be driven by Chinese companies: state media valued the domestic dexterous hand industry last year as worth more than 50bn yuan (£5.6bn).

Walker doesn’t like to use the word “competition” when talking about these companies. Ever the robot enthusiast, he sees them as working towards a common good. “There will be breakthroughs that suddenly just move everything forward. That might be a better motor, it might be a polymer that makes a skin that is better, it might be a way of sensing the world that lets the robot understand things in a way that we haven’t been able to do before at scale in a cheap robot.” He pauses. “It’s exciting.”

“Shadow is in a difficult position,” Nathan Lepora, professor of robotics and AI at the University of Bristol, tells me in a video call. “The Shadow Hand was best in class for 20 years, but it’s the price of a Lamborghini. Now there are a lot of very capable hands for the price of a Vauxhall. China is going through a massive expansion of hand development, and at the beginning of this decade you would never have predicted the level of dexterity that we’re seeing today.”

When I ask Lepora how close he thinks we are to developing a robot hand that can rival a human’s, he tells me that’s not the point. “We don’t necessarily need the robots to do all that hands can do. We want them to be able to pick up and manipulate objects and tools.” The current crop of robot hands might not be at that point yet, but they’re close, he says. “We’ve got a good chance of seeing general tool use by the end of this decade.”

I tell Lepora about the Amazon workers I saw in the fulfilment centre, who aren’t required to use any tools – they just have to be able to stow, pick and pack a wide variety of objects. “Their days are numbered,” he says, simply. “They are the last bits that haven’t yet been automated.” Amazon must already be working on replacing them, he adds. “I’m sure they are close to it.” Production lines without any human workers are part of manufacturing today: China has fully automated “dark factories” – so called because they can operate with the lights off – that run 24/7.

If the future looks bleak for Amazon workers, what about manual labourers in general? When I mention retraining as a plumber for job security in the age of AI, Lepora shoots me a look as if to say, don’t be naive. “Maybe for 10 or 15 years. Plumbing’s not going to be done by a robot this decade, that’s for sure. But after then?”

In Shadow Robot HQ, Walker argues that plumbers are here to stay for the foreseeable future. They have to apply themselves – and the available tools – to such a wide variety of unusual spaces and problems, after all; their skill comes from being adaptable, not from knowing the correct way to perform a procedure, he says. A dexterous hand alone will not take their job. “If you’ve ever seen a plumber get under your bath and do something to the tap at the back, you’ll realise that’s going to be a job for a humanoid robot at best.”

But on its website, the company say it is “working towards robotics for a safer world by allowing robots to enter extreme environments where it would be too risky for a human to go. This includes jobs that are too dull, dirty, difficult, dexterous, dangerous, and/or dear.” Walker and his team might be determined to build “robots for good”, but if they manage to get everything on that list right, they will eliminate much of human manual labour.

When I put this to him, he stiffens. He’d clearly much rather be talking about motors and tendon load sensors than the social and economic implications of where his hands might reach.

“If we solved all of the things on that list then that would be amazing, but I think that that’s several hundred years’ work for several hundred organisations and several hundred major breakthroughs will have to happen for that to happen,” he says. “Is what we’re doing likely to lead to the doom of humanity? That sounds like a marketing campaign. If I wanted to increase my share value, I’d probably say, yes, we’re going to lead to the doom of humanity – invest in us.”

No one likes to think that their job could be taken by a robot – not fulfilment centre workers, nor plumbers, nor journalists. What about Alistair Hunter, the hand surgeon? It’s hard to think of a profession that demands as much of a combination of knowledge and dexterity – brain plus hand – than his.

“When I’m operating, there are times where I’m at the very limit of my manual dexterity and my understanding. Is it possible for a robot to learn that amount of experience that I’ve developed over many years and then action it autonomously? I think that would be very difficult,” Hunter replies. “I don’t think you can ever say ‘impossible’, because 50 years ago I wouldn’t have anticipated anything of what’s possible now. But knowing what I do about the hand, and knowing what I do about surgery, I think that would be a very difficult thing to do.”

It’s easy to imagine that, in a world of embodied AI, it would be a safer bet to become a robotics engineer than a surgeon. But the nature of our work is changing so rapidly, and no career is necessarily safe.

Ultimately, Lepora says, robot hands will be making robot hands. “I don’t think any company is at that pivot point yet, but that’s where we’re ending up.” If and when that happens, robot hands will be cheaper than ever – and advancing at an extraordinary pace. “You could produce them at scale, but you could also automate the improvement of them as well,” he tells me, leaning forward with excitement. “Once they can build them themselves, you iterate it. That is the possible tipping point for when the hands will become really, really capable.” It’s also the point where robot engineers themselves might be out of a job.

headline: ‘I ain’t goin nowhere’: Gullah Geechee people fight off developers with a historic referendum
body:
