Ire Gene Grovner stood behind his house on a recent morning, between chicken pens on one side and rows of winter collard greens on the other, holding a knife and skinning a raccoon splayed across a wood post.

“The meat is good roasted,” Grovner said. He pointed to the collards, a burst of green in the winter cold, and the chickens, with their eggs. “If you ain’t lazy, you can live good here,” he said, referring to Sapelo Island off the coast of southern Georgia.

Then he waved in a broad circle, pointing out the nearby modest homes of family members, all bearing the same last name as him, which Grovner, who is 70, says stretches nine generations back on Hogg Hummock.

The community is home to the Gullah Geechee people, descendants of enslaved west Africans who worked on cotton, indigo and rice plantations from North Carolina to Florida. In places like South Carolina’s Hilton Head Island, the Gullah Geechee population was nearly wiped out by development starting in the 1960s.

On Sapelo Island, post-enslavement, freed Black folks were granted land in Hogg Hummock in part because it was seen as marshy and less desirable than the rest of the island. It is the only remaining sea island community of Gullah Geechee people in Georgia.
full:
A citizen referendum, only the second of its kind in Georgia history, seeks to block a zoning amendment

Ire Gene Grovner stood behind his house on a recent morning, between chicken pens on one side and rows of winter collard greens on the other, holding a knife and skinning a raccoon splayed across a wood post.

“The meat is good roasted,” Grovner said. He pointed to the collards, a burst of green in the winter cold, and the chickens, with their eggs. “If you ain’t lazy, you can live good here,” he said, referring to Sapelo Island off the coast of southern Georgia.

Then he waved in a broad circle, pointing out the nearby modest homes of family members, all bearing the same last name as him, which Grovner, who is 70, says stretches nine generations back on Hogg Hummock.

The community is home to the Gullah Geechee people, descendants of enslaved west Africans who worked on cotton, indigo and rice plantations from North Carolina to Florida. In places like South Carolina’s Hilton Head Island, the Gullah Geechee population was nearly wiped out by development starting in the 1960s.

On Sapelo Island, post-enslavement, freed Black folks were granted land in Hogg Hummock in part because it was seen as marshy and less desirable than the rest of the island. It is the only remaining sea island community of Gullah Geechee people in Georgia.

“All that’s family,” Grovner summed up. “All those people who want to build houses here ain’t gonna close me in.”

Outsiders building large vacation houses was what was at stake in Tuesday’s election in McIntosh county, where Sapelo is located – only the second citizen referendum on a county plan or policy in Georgia history. (Nearby Camden county voters defeated a county plan to build a rocket-launching pad through a referendum in 2022.)

The referendum, brought about after more than 2,000 registered voters in the county signed petitions, allowed residents to vote on whether they were for or against a zoning amendment increasing the amount of residential square footage permitted in Hogg Hummock from 1,400 to 3,000.

Unofficial results released on Tuesday evening showed that nearly 85% of 1,869 county voters opposed the zoning increase.

Allowing larger houses to be built on the island would have opened the door to developers – “all those people” Grovner named – which then would raise taxes, making it harder for Gullah Geechee people to continue living on Sapelo, and potentially changing the island’s cultural and environmental landscape forever.

The number of Gullah Geechee people living on Sapelo has dwindled to between 30 and 40 residents, down from about 500 in the early 20th century. Dozens of the residents’ children and other family members have moved to the mainland over time. Nonetheless, many of these family members maintain ties to the island; some still own property and plan on retiring there.

“Every county in the state of Georgia is looking at” Tuesday’s results, said Kathleen Russell, editor of the Darien News – because any county’s residents can now mount a referendum and challenge zoning rules, she said.

The referendum made history in the region as well, as referendums “are incredibly rare in the majority of the south”, said Chris Melody Fields Figueredo, executive director of the Ballot Initiative Strategy Center. The reason: “States where formerly enslaved people lived, the state governments did not want those people to exercise their power,” Fields Figueredo said.

The ability to stage a referendum in Georgia comes from provisions in the state’s constitution. First, a certain percentage of a county’s registered voters signs a petition indicating they want to vote on a policy from the county’s elected representatives. The percentage varies based on the county’s population.

Once the threshold of confirmed signatures is reached and a referendum is authorized, it is “a form of holding power accountable, where systems of governance are challenged”, said Fields Figueredo.

The Gullah Geechee people who were leading the effort to hold the referendum first had to defeat the county’s legal challenges, based on assertions that zoning rules weren’t covered by language in the state’s constitution. It took a September state supreme court decision to give the green light to Tuesday’s election.

The Guardian spoke to a handful of the nearly 1,000 county residents who cast ballots during a two-week early voting period ending Friday. All had ties to Sapelo Island and Hogg Hummock, and felt strongly about the need to protect the community from unchecked development.

The unspoiled qualities that allow Gullah Geechee people to live close to nature also make the island a prime location for natural science; in the 1950s, Sapelo was the site of foundational research in the nascent field of ecology.

After casting his ballot on Thursday, Nick Macías described Sapelo as “an ecologically important island you don’t find anywhere in the world”. Macías, who works as assistant operations director at the island’s University of Georgia Marine Institute, pointed out that Sapelo was the only Georgia sea island with healthy communities of marsh grass – a keystone species, or one that other animals and plants in an ecosystem depend on for survival.

after newsletter promotion

Allowing larger houses and increased development in Hogg Hummock “would put stress on the carbon footprint” of the island and displace Gullah Geechee people, he said: “When it comes to preserving the [Gullah Geechee] culture, it comes down to the next generation being able to live there.”

Also voting last week, Samuel – who didn’t want his last name used – had gotten off his job early as a trucker to cast a ballot. He has ties to Hogg Hummock through his wife, who has family there. “It’s a unique place,” he said. “You go there … and they treat you like family. They take you in.”

The trucker remembers first visiting as a teenager. “They showed me medicine for toothaches, using plants,” he said. As for the community’s ongoing struggles, he said, “I’ll fight for it till the end. They deserve it. It’s their place.”

One of Ire Gene Grovner’s relatives in Hogg Hummock is his brother, Bobby Gene Grovner. He’s renovating his home on the island, with plans of leaving it to his two daughters. “These ones who come with a pocketful of money, it ain’t gonna work,” he said, referring to developers with interest in the community’s land.

Still, Bobby Gene, who turns 67 later this month, said “it’s tiring” to have to fight in courtrooms and government halls for his community.

“I ain’t got but 40 years left!” he said, laughing.

His brother Ire Gene is involved in another unresolved legal battle, laying claim to several dozen acres of land that a 2024 lawsuit asserts was taken from his family by the state of Georgia in nearby Raccoon Bluff, a 698-acre plot of land on the island formerly inhabited by Gullah Geechee people. The lawsuit includes land deed records in Grovner’s family dating to 1875.

An ongoing case involving the subject of Tuesday’s referendum, filed by the Southern Poverty Law Center, asserts that the proposed zoning amendment was discriminatory. “The people in [Hogg Hummock] feel like they’ve been shut out,” said the SPLC attorney Miriam Gutman. “[They] want to pass their land onto their children and grandchildren. They want to be part of the conversation” about the community’s future, she said.

But even the immediate future after Tuesday’s result is unclear, as the McIntosh county attorney, Adam Poppell, recently stated that voters rejecting the county’s attempt to increase the maximum square footage allowed on the island doesn’t mean conditions will revert to what they were before: a limit of 1,400 sq ft. Instead, Poppell said, the election’s result leaves Hogg Hummock with “no zoning” – meaning anything could be built.

The county attorney did not answer a request for comment.

Dana Braun, attorney for the Hogg Hummock residents who mounted the referendum effort, said another lawsuit would be likely if the county insists on Poppell’s interpretation of where things stand. “The county apparently loves paying lawyers for losing battles,” he said.

After cleaning off his knife and preparing the raccoon on Friday, Ire Gene turned to face the chicken pens and the morning’s eggs. His position on the future of Hogg Hummock: “I ain’t planning on goin’ nowhere.”

headline: ‘A new record for entertainment’: Grand Theft Auto VI sales hit $3.8bn on first day of release, developer says
body:
The announcement from Rockstar Games would mean GTA VI has already earned more than the entire box office run of the highest-grossing film of all time

Grand Theft Auto VI generated $3.79bn in retail sales on its first day, publisher Rockstar Games has announced, calling it the biggest launch for any entertainment product in history.

The worldwide figure was based on company estimates through the end of the day Thursday, the day the game launched. Rockstar said also it had sold 32.5m units of the game on prerelease, setting a record across platforms.

“We are incredibly humbled by the response from players around the world and we couldn’t be more excited to share this moment with you,” Sam Houser, Rockstar’s president and founder, said in a statement.

The company said the sales set “a new record for entertainment across any medium … becoming the biggest entertainment launch in history.”

The figure is nearly five times the roughly $800m that predecessor Grand Theft Auto V attracted during its first 24 hours in 2013.

It also exceeds the entire box office run of Avengers: Endgame, which became the highest-grossing film of all time last month at about $2.9bn worldwide after a rerelease pushed it past Avatar.

The game went on sale Thursday on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, launching first in New Zealand and rolling out market by market as each reached midnight local time.

The game went on sale Thursday on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, launching first in New Zealand and rolling out market by market as each reached midnight local time.

The release quickly became a global phenomenon, generating more social media posts than this year’s World Cup, according to monitoring platform Visibrain.

Critics praised the game, which has a score of 99 on review aggregator Metacritic.

Rockstar said that made it the highest-rated game ever.

Like its predecessors, “GTA VI” is an open-world action game in which players roam freely through a sprawling city, stealing cars, pulling off heists and carrying out missions for criminal gangs.

Its busy streets, neon-lit nightlife and beaches are rendered in striking detail, and non-player characters go about their lives whether or not the player is involved.

While critics have raved about the game, it has also prompted real-world warnings from authorities.

With the game’s release on Thursday, police departments across the US reminded people that the car thefts, reckless driving, violence and other criminal mayhem depicted in the blockbuster title should not be re-enacted on the country’s streets.

There is insufficient evidence supporting a scientific causal link between violent video games and violent behaviour, according to the American Psycyhological Association. Nonetheless, several police departments took to the internet with warnings – and even jokes – aimed at keeping GTA VI’s lawlessness firmly in the virtual world.

The Atlanta police department delivered one of the clearest messages in a social media post.

“GTA is not a real place, but Atlanta is!” the department warned. “Don’t confuse virtual entertainment with real-life decisions.”

headline: CEO of funding agency for UK science and research criticised by union over cuts
body:

Exclusive: Prospect’s Mike Clancy tells Ian Chapman at UKRI that union has ‘lost confidence’ in his leadership

A trade union that counts scientists and engineers among its members says it has lost confidence in the leader of the UK’s national funding agency for science and research, citing concerns about plans for major cuts.

The letter from Mike Clancy, the general secretary of Prospect, to Ian Chapman, the chief executive of UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), is the latest development in a row over changes in funding for projects and research facilities.

“Writing to a CEO in this tone and to this intent is an extraordinary step for this union to have to take,” Clancy wrote.

He warned: “Whilst there are legitimate cost pressures facing UKRI, ultimately any cuts will reduce the UK’s national science capability at a time when it is most needed.”

This year the Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC), the government’s infrastructure funding agency, which is part of UKRI, revealed it needed to make £162m in savings by 2030.

While the core budget of the STFC remains broadly flat at about £835m a year, it is under financial pressure as a result of several factors. These include soaring energy costs at its national facilities, increasing staffing costs, an expanded portfolio of activities and “unfavourable movements” in foreign exchange rates. The last has resulted in an increase in costs relating to international facilities such as Cern.

As a result, in July UKRI released a plan to balance the STFC’s budget by 2030, revealing research projects and national facilities are to face significant changes.

“As responsible custodians of public funds, which I very much view our job is to be, we have to make sure that our costs are in line with our budget and that we don’t overspend the budget available to us,” Chapman said at the time, adding that it was important to prioritise spending in areas that made the biggest scientific impact.

The future of the UK’s largest telescope at the Jodrell Bank Observatory in Cheshire has been put at risk, while the Diamond Light Source, the Central Laser Facility and the Isis Neutron and Muon Source, all in Oxfordshire, will remain operational but have been told to make efficiency savings.

The Clara facility in Cheshire – one of the world’s most advanced medium-energy electron beam facilities, which develops and tests next-generation accelerator technologies – is to be mothballed.

Clancy wrote in his letter to Chapman: “Our members working at UKRI do vital work which puts our country at the cutting edge of scientific developments and industrial applications and has considerable benefits across high-growth sectors, as well as in medical research and treatment. To pause or ‘mothball’ funding for many of the facilities where they work is to risk permanently losing the expertise that underpins the sector.”

The opening of a voluntary exit scheme to UKRI employees was also flagged by Clancy, who said the scheme was launched in parallel with the STFC cuts and without the requisite consultation on the organisational change plan with the recognised trade unions. His letter urges a pause to enable proper consultation and evidence-gathering on the cuts’ potential impact.

“In the absence of our requests leading to any productive engagement, we have lost confidence in your position as CEO,” Clancy wrote to Chapman.

Prof Leszek Borysiewicz, the chair of UKRI, said the board had full confidence in Chapman and his leadership team.

“We support the direction of the ambitious reform programme UKRI is undertaking to become more effective, agile and better able to respond to the country’s priorities and needs,” Borysiewicz said. “Delivering transformation on this scale is a substantial undertaking involving difficult decisions about how UKRI operates, where resources are focused and how we deliver the greatest impact.

“UKRI has been clear with staff and unions about the direction of change, including its new mission and funding model, greater join-up across programmes and the unification of professional services. The decisions announced this year followed extensive engagement with staff, research and user communities, alongside detailed consideration of the impacts of different funding choices.” The science minister, Chris McDonald, said: “I have full confidence in Ian Chapman’s leadership of UKRI. The organisation’s ongoing and essential transformation programme will ensure projects supported through our record £86bn commitment to R&D will deliver maximum impact and value for money – as the British public rightly expect.

“I know from personal experience that this transformation will have a significant and personal impact on workers and others affected, and we will continue to engage the UKRI workforce. I am committed to working closely with UKRI, the workers, and their trade unions as we continue to progress the transformation plan.”

headline: Financial bullying can ruin a marriage: first-person stories
body:
When partners consider finances, when is it ‘my’ money, and when it is ‘our’ money? Guardian readers shared their experiences

A survey of about 1,000 Americans found that one in 10 would describe their partner as a financial bully. Our readers, however, insist that that might be a label easily assigned to a partner who is simply being financially responsible.

When we put out a call to out readers last week to see if any of them had similar experiences, we found that many of you wouldn’t define the actions described as financial bullying. Instead, quite a number of you insisted that keeping track of your partner’s expenses was simply budgeting and being financially responsible.

Adam: “Having disagreements about spending in a relationship is hardly bullying, it is natural and unavoidable and has happened since the dawn of money.”

Rebecca: “I thought it was called teaching financial responsibility.”

Sean: “Families should work together to maintain a budget, often one spouse is more reckless than the other, that’s not bullying, that’s being responsible.”

Sarah: “Financial bullying?! Sharing a life together and a bank account means both parties get to be involved in spending decisions.”

Nicole: “My husband knows how much money I spend. From a certain amount, I always ask him, if he’s OK with it. I won’t call it ‘financial bullying’, I call it ‘living together’. Someone has to keep an eye on the family’s money.”

Okay... but in all fairness, if you have a joint back account, and a budget, and one member of the party goes out and spends $250 unannounced on some superfluous item, then that's worthy of a conversation. And monitoring how much both people are spending is good practice.

There's nothing wrong with checking in, making sure that both parties in a relationship know how much they can spend on XY or Z.

I often look at charges and ask my husband what they are. Mostly, to make sure that anything unusual is not fraud. Secondly, if there is a huge charge for something we didn't discuss, to make sure he knows what our budget is and to stay within it. My husband often does not know what is in our bank account, flies off on work, spends a large amount of money on dinner and drinks, and then leaves me scrimping on grocery bills.

Does that make me a bully if I check our balance and warn him if his spending is going over the budget? You know, we also have rent and food to pay for, and only one bank account between us, of which I am the larger earner. My husband should feel ashamed if he blows our budget on expensive meals or jeans. Just as I should feel ashamed if I go out on a shopping spree that prevents us from buying food. Where does necessary budgeting and monitoring end, and bullying begin?

My ex-husband routinely spent our rent/bill/food money on restaurants, taxis and other things we really didn’t have the budget for. Finally I got sick of being behind on rent and always running out of money for food, and put my foot down. He refused to sit down and do a budget with me, saying “Why don’t you just do it?” So I did.

I made a budget of all his personal spending, and finally I had to make him choose between taxis to work and lunch at restaurants, which felt bizarre and incredibly uncomfortable for me. He chose taxis over lunch, and after that, whenever colleagues would ask him why he wasn’t joining them for lunch, he’d tell them that his wife wouldn’t allow it.

So my question is, who was the financial bully in this situation, me or him?

A reader from Arkansas says she was financially bullied by her then-husband for years:

But not the way you mean: when I suggested he cut back on his credit-card use on the card held in my name, he sharply increased his use, increasing our debt to $23,000 in a matter of months. That’s what I call financial bullying.

Even checking the accounts doesn’t stop financial ruin:

A few years after we were married, my ex-husband developed a drug abuse problem. I was balancing the checkbook every month. He would take money out of our accounts to buy and sell drugs and not tell me. When the accounts wouldn’t match up, he would berate me for not being accurate. He spent all of our money and ran the credit cards up to the max.

When we got divorced we had two credit cards, one for the home and one for his “business” that never got off the ground. The agreement was that I would pay off the family card and he would pay off the business card. Of course, he never did and the creditors came after me – I wound up paying both of them off. My credit was wrecked for seven years.

Reading the comments here I guess none of the commentators has experienced this.

I have and it certainly was bullying. Talking about finances together is very different from keeping a tight eye on your partner’s spending and questioning every last penny. In my situation, this was coupled with a wholly one-sided approach to discussing joint spending which characterised what I suggested as ‘spending on me’ while what they wanted as ‘spending on us’.

Unless you’ve been in that sort of relationship, I recommend that you aren’t so quick to judge.

Been there too. Money I earned was “our money”, money she earned was “her money”. She was serious. She would get hysterical whenever I bought a magazine yet she felt she could blow hundreds in one shopping spree on whatever she felt like having.

A female reader living in New York wrote:

I am in an arranged marriage, to a man who is self-made after a struggled childhood, with disregarded needs, as defined above. However, unless purchases are made to his own liking, he is extremely tight with money. For many years into my marriage – around five – I had no say in the type of food I ate or clothes I wore. My request for a choice of three types of breakfast cereals was seen as “an attempt to cremate his money”. My clothes came from Walmart or Value City.

When we went out, I was expected to eat at home, and could not have a $1 coffee or $1 hot dog in case I got a little peckish under the guise of ‘saving money’ and ‘aggressive savings targets’. If an eggplant spoiled in the refrigerator, the spoiled part was taken and smeared across my face and down my arms, to teach me the value of money. The rear of the television set was checked for warmth on arrival home from work to prove I had been watching TV all day and therefore ‘wasting electricity’. My grocery shopping was severely monitored, as I ‘made it my mission to waste money’.

I think it is important to note I had no earnings of my own during this period.

Fast-forward many years. Now I have my own earnings. My favorite shops are Nordstrom and Anthropologie [where I shop] on the regular and hide [purchases] in the closet. [I] accuse [my] better half of a bad memory when the clothes, bags and shoes make an appearance – with no apologies or regret whatsoever for my behaviours!

However, I think it’s fair to say that we have a sizeable bank balance and the mortgage is a year from being paid off in full.

headline: Millions of Spaniards stage general strike
body:
First general strike since workers downed tools in 2012 against austerity measures during the euro zone debt crisis

Four million Spanish workers took part in a general strike on Wednesday, unions said, enduring stormy weather to set up picket lines in a protest against the country's housing affordability crisis less than three weeks before a snap general election.

It is the first general strike since workers downed tools in 2012 against austerity measures during the euro zone debt crisis. The walkout is backed by Spain's two largest unions, UGT and CCOO, representing more than a million workers, as well as tenants' associations angry about rising rents and evictions.

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez hopes to harness voter resentment over housing in the November 29 election to shift the political narrative away from corruption cases involving his inner circle and a deadly train crash last month. So far, his Socialist Party trails in opinion polls.

headline: SOEs scrap LPG auctions after LHC intervention
body:
Distributors challenge federal guidelines shifting price-setting powers from OGRA to SOEs

The LPG auctions planned by state-owned enterprises (SOEs) Oil and Gas Development Company Limited (OGDCL), Pakistan Petroleum Limited (PPL) and Pak-Arab Refinery Limited (PARCO) have been scrapped, the Pakistan LPG Marketers Association (PLPGMA) announced. The SOEs confirmed this before the Lahore High Court (LHC) on November 20.

The PLPGMA had filed Writ Petition No 45981 of 2026 challenging the auction notices and Invitations to Bids issued under advertisements dated July 26, 2026. The association argued that the proposed process was contrary to the legal and regulatory framework governing the LPG sector that prohibits LPG producers from charging any sort of premium over and above the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (OGRA) notified price. OGRA and the Federation of Pakistan were named as Respondents 1 and 2.

On August 7, 2026, the LHC suspended the auction process. When the matter was heard on November 20, counsel for OGDCL, PPL and PARCO stated before the court that the auctions had been scrapped. As the immediate relief sought had been achieved, the PLPGMA's counsel consented to the withdrawal of the petition, and the court disposed of it. "This outcome confirms that LPG sector decisions must follow the established legal and regulatory framework," a PLPGMA spokesperson said.

headline: COP31 venue failed the disability access challenge
body:
COP31 participants criticise poor accessibility, citing unmarked floors and inadequate sign language services

On days she attended COP31, the annual UN climate conference, Süheyla Doğan walked a kilometer with a cane from the tram station to the Blue Zone, passing through the entrance. The 69-year-old activist, known for leading ecological protection efforts in Türkiye’s Kazdağları region, says there should have been some effort to ensure that attendees with mobility issues have access to a shuttle from the tram stop to the Blue Zone. To reach the Blue Zone, people had to walk up one pedestrian bridge, climb down, and then climb up and down a second pedestrian bridge — roughly a kilometer on foot in crowds that don’t usually stop or give space. “Everyone rushed to get in,” she noted.

Doğan managed to get a wheelchair from the accessibility counter at the COP31 venue, which was manned by an overwhelmingly local Turkish staff. But while the wheelchair allowed her to navigate the sprawling venue to a certain extent, it did not quite help her at the end of her day. “The wheelchair had to be returned before the exit at the venue,” she said with visible frustration. Inside, she pointed to a lack of space for wheelchairs in a crowd of an estimated 100,000 attendees, delegates, negotiators, and observers.

COP31 participants criticise poor accessibility, citing unmarked floors and inadequate sign language services

On days she attended COP31, the annual UN climate conference, Süheyla Doğan walked a kilometer with a cane from the tram station to the Blue Zone, passing through the entrance. The 69-year-old activist, known for leading ecological protection efforts in Türkiye’s Kazdağları region, says there should have been some effort to ensure that attendees with mobility issues have access to a shuttle from the tram stop to the Blue Zone. To reach the Blue Zone, people had to walk up one pedestrian bridge, climb down, and then climb up and down a second pedestrian bridge — roughly a kilometer on foot in crowds that don’t usually stop or give space. “Everyone rushed to get in,” she noted.

Doğan managed to get a wheelchair from the accessibility counter at the COP31 venue, which was manned by an overwhelmingly local Turkish staff. But while the wheelchair allowed her to navigate the sprawling venue to a certain extent, it did not quite help her at the end of her day. “The wheelchair had to be returned before the exit at the venue,” she said with visible frustration. Inside, she pointed to a lack of space for wheelchairs in a crowd of an estimated 100,000 attendees, delegates, negotiators, and observers.

Della Leonor, a disability advocate from the Philippines, confirmed a similarly exhausting daily journey. “Well I had a great challenge because from the hotel we have to walk to the bus stop everyday,” she said. “There was a slope from the exit down to the road, after that the road had humps, and a wheelchair needed to be carried to access the bus. Upon arrival sometimes volunteers pushed us up the venue, but more often my personal assistant pushed me the whole way. It was so tiring, and having a wheelchair is a big challenge.” Her suggestions were direct: “The bus should have fetched participants directly from the hotel exit. A separate route should have been provided for persons with disabilities.”

The official record describes something very different. Turkish state-linked outlets reported that the entire 1.1 million square metre Blue and Green Zone was “planned as accessible,” supported by a 114-person Accessibility Team, 102 of them volunteers in purple vests, assigned to 521 registered disabled delegates. For physical access, organizers reported deploying 77 wheelchairs (61 manual, 16 battery-powered), alongside guide paths, Braille markings, tactile maps, and audio guidance for blind and low-vision attendees. For deaf participants, the Ministry of Family and Social Services assigned 30 sign language interpreters who worked across 31 different halls at the venue. Organizers also stated that seven Quiet Rooms were available for attendees with sensory sensitivities, and that 69 guests had been directed to them. Mustafa Ertok, COP31’s accessibility lead, was quoted saying that “we have met the needs of all 521 participants, both in transportation and within the venue,” and that accessibility was being treated “not as a preference, but as a human right”.

But the official COP31 accessibility page itself, as of the scheduled final day of the conference, was still publishing placeholders. Quiet and decompression spaces were “being explored,” with information to be provided “if these spaces are confirmed” (cop31.tr/accessibility). Sign language interpretation arrangements were “being coordinated with the relevant authorities,” with session-by-session details promised only “once arrangements are finalized”. These are not descriptions of services already delivered, they are prospective commitments, published while the conference was underway, for provisions that disabled attendees were told to expect.

Clare Gibellini, an Equality at Work Ambassador and policy leader advancing the rights, inclusion and employment of women with disabilities, who attended COP31 representing the National Disability Research Partnership (NDRP), Australia, assessed the same arrangements in a word that leaves no room for diplomatic ambiguity: “Honestly, they failed. Not partially, not ‘could do better.’ They failed.”

Gibellini’s account directly contradicts the official inventory at every layer. “There was no closed captioning, no sign language interpretation, and no quiet spaces anywhere in the venue,” she said. For blind and low-vision attendees, information was “not being provided in accessible formats,” and she specifically flagged the absence of Easy Read or plain language materials, meaning people with intellectual disabilities or low literacy were “shut out of the very documents and announcements that shape their futures.” On mobility, she pointed to the same first-mile failure Doğan described: “Wheelchair users are struggling to even get to the venue because the transport is not accessible.” And for sensory access, the pavilions were “so noisy that people with sensory or hearing impairments simply cannot participate.”

A blind attendee from the Global South, who spoke on condition of anonymity, described a further gap that official claims of tactile maps and Braille markings did not address. The entire pavilion area where booths were set up lacked any floor markings for visually impaired participants, no tactile strips, no Braille signage on the ground, no guided path through the exhibition space. “I could not visit the pavilions at all,” the attendee said. “There was no way to know where anything was, no way to find the booths I had come to see. The guide paths the organizers talk about did not extend into the areas that mattered most for networking and learning.” The account directly contradicts the official claim that guide paths and tactile maps were in place all over the venue. While such measures did exist at entry points or along main corridors, they did not reach the pavilion floors where the substantive exchanges of COP31 took place.

Gibellini framed the failure not as a logistical oversight but as a human rights problem. Both Türkiye and Australia have ratified the Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities, which obligates states to ensure accessible information and the full participation of disabled people in public and political life. “A summit that decides the future of our planet, while locking out the people most affected by climate change, is not an inclusive summit,” she said. "It is a summit that has decided whose participation matters and whose does not.”

She described accessibility as operating on three layers, and said COP31 “essentially missed that entire layer” of practical accommodations, ramps, captions, interpreters, accessible formats, and quiet spaces. The second layer is the cost transferred onto disabled people themselves: the energy, the planning, the recovery time, the extra support required “just to get through a venue that was not built for them.” The third is attitudes, whether organizers treat lived experience as expertise or as “a box to tick.” The message from the setup of this COP, she said, is that “our participation was never really planned for.”

Her recommendations for UNFCCC were concrete: make accessibility standards a condition of hosting, verified through a published pre-conference audit; co-design with disabled persons’ organisations and establish a complaints mechanism so barriers are fixed “in days, not years”; make captioning, interpretation, Easy Read, and quiet rooms the default, backed by a dedicated budget line; and recognise the Disability Caucus as a formal constituency within the UNFCCC. “Inclusion that only works for non-disabled bodies is not inclusion,” she said.

The gap between the official numbers and the lived accounts is not merely a matter of degree. It is a gap between provision on paper and access in practice. The International Disability Alliance, at its Disability Climate Caucus press conference at COP31, made the same point in structural terms: “Accessibility cannot be limited to physical access alone. Persons with disabilities must be able to meaningfully participate, influence decisions, and shape climate policies that directly affect their lives and communities.” Reporting from the ground noted that even where sign language interpretation was nominally available, it was offered only in select sessions and required 48 hours' advance request, a procedural barrier that undermines the very purpose of on-demand access.

The Express Tribune approached the UNFCCC office, the media desk at the venue, and the press office, including Tim Davis, Manager of the International Broadcast Centre (IBC) of the UNFCCC, for comment on the accessibility arrangements. Despite repeated reminders both in person and over e-mail, no response was provided. The accessibility desk set up at the front of the venue not only declined to comment, Can Ergün, a staff member deployed there, became hostile to any sort of inquiry. The UNFCCC remained silent on questions about the number of wheelchairs present at the venue until the end of the conference. But activists and attendees at the disability caucus were not muted about their concerns. The official record will show that 77 wheelchairs were deployed, 30 interpreters assigned, and seven quiet rooms designated. What it will not show is the kilometer Doğan walked on a cane, the wheelchair she had to return before she could leave, the bus Della Leonor could not reach without being carried over road humps, the pavilion floors that offered no path for a blind attendee, or the Accessibility Help Desk that turned them, and the journalists asking about them, away.

"As soon as she tries to enter Bangladesh, she will be arrested. And she will be taken to jail, and the law will take its course," Obaed said in an interview on Sunday. "We would like India to honour the extradition treaty and return her as a convict, and the law will take its course. She (Hasina) will have to face the music."

The standoff has brought Hasina's Awami League supporters out on the streets. The party this month announced a week of protests and rallies in support of Hasina's return, culminating in a nationwide lockdown on November 19.

Police have recorded dozens of crude bomb blasts and incidents of arson targeting vehicles in at least 28 districts over the past 10 days, with several police officers and civilians injured, according to local media.

Obaed called the violence a survival tactic by Hasina's "politically bankrupt political party."

Khalid Mahmud Chowdhury, a senior Awami League official, said the current political establishment was responsible for the violence. The minister said there had been no official discussions with India about sending an aircraft to bring Hasina back, adding that Dhaka wanted balanced ties with New Delhi that did not compromise Bangladesh's "dignity, self-respect and interests."

"India needs to decide what kind of foreign policy they need to adopt for Bangladesh," Obaed said.

Dhaka is also stepping up diplomatic pressure on neighbouring Myanmar over the return of Rohingya refugees after the UN's highest court ruled that thousands of killings and widespread sexual violence by Myanmar's security forces against the Muslim minority in 2017 amounted to state-sponsored genocide.

Myanmar has criticised the ruling by the International ‌Court of Justice said Rohingya would only be able to return "when situations permit".

"Now, this verdict gives us, Bangladesh, the strength, the Rohingya community the strength to fight," Obaed said, adding that they deserved to return "with dignity and safety".

About 1.2 million Rohingya live in Bangladesh after repeated repatriation attempts failed. Their return has been complicated by Myanmar's civil war and the Arakan Army militia's control of nearly all of Rakhine State, which is home for most Rohingya.

Obaed called for greater international pressure on Myanmar and the Arakan Army. "Bangladesh did not create this crisis. Myanmar created this crisis, so Myanmar has to end it," she said.

headline: Rosenior warns Paris FC to focus as they climb second in Ligue 1
body:
The newly promoted side move three points behind PSG after recording their biggest win of the season

Paris FC coach Liam Rosenior welcomed his side's rise to second in Ligue 1 after a 4-0 win over Angers on Sunday, but insisted it was too early to draw any longer-term conclusions.

With 11 games gone, Paris FC trail Paris Saint-Germain by three points while Lille have 21.

Against Angers, Paris FC's Ivorian forward Patrick Zabi broke the deadlock in the 47th minute and Luca Koleosho doubled the lead on 55, both from assists by Diego Coppola.

Maxime Lopez made it 3-0 on the hour mark and defender Coppola completed the scoring himself with his first goal since May 2025 to seal an emphatic 4-0 victory.

"I'm very pleased with the team's current position in the table. But no matter in football or in life, you mustn't get carried away. We need to stay focused on each match," said former Chelsea player Rosenior, who took over at Paris FC in the close season.

Rosenior brushed aside talk of a December 12 derby against leaders PSG.

"They are probably the best team in the world right now. We have enormous respect for what they are achieving and what they represent. We have three important matches to play before we even start thinking about PSG," the English coach said.

headline: Farmers to get access to AI in daily lives
body:
Parliamentary Secretary says they will be able to forecast their yields and productivity

The government of Punjab is working towards incorporating artificial intelligence (AI) into the daily lives of farmers as the provincial leadership believes in data and technological revolution. This was stated by Parliamentary Secretary Osama Leghari while speaking at the Pakistan Agricultural Coalition's Agri Connections Conference and Expo on Thursday.

"I hope that during the remaining two and a half years of our tenure, we will successfully lay the foundation through which our farmers will have access to AI and will be able to forecast their yields and productivity," said Leghari.

headline: New Zealand dig deep to deny India victory in Wellington thriller

Mitchell and Phillips hold firm to secure a hard-fought draw

New Zealand rescued a draw on the final day of the first Test against India in Wellington on Monday, surviving 120 overs in a fighting display to finish 239-5 at the close.

India had declared their first innings on a mammoth 720-9 midway through the fourth day with a lead of 352 runs after New Zealand made 368.

Daryl Mitchell (49 not out) and Glenn Phillips (26 not out) batted India into submission on a lifeless Basin Reserve pitch.

The two-Test series moves to Christchurch on Friday with all to play for in the decider.

"You know, we're pretty happy," New Zealand captain Tom Latham said of the draw.

"Obviously India played fantastically well. We were under pressure, only a couple of results at play and to be in the position where a couple of guys put their hands up was great."

India had needed five wickets in the final session for victory, but there were few alarms for the New Zealand batsmen.

Captain Shubman Gill shook hands with Phillips and Mitchell an hour before the scheduled close to agree a draw after turning to part-time bowlers Yashasvi Jaiswal and Dhruv Jurel in a last, desperate attempt for a breakthrough.

"All of our fast bowlers bowled almost 50 overs in the match," Gill said of his decision.

headline: UN climate chief urges faster action at COP31
body:
Wars and inflation push climate change down governments' priority lists

The UN's top climate official urged negotiators at the COP31 conference in Turkey on Saturday to move swiftly towards a deal and "avoid tactical delays" as the summit heads into its second and final week.

The annual UN climate conference faces new challenges this year as a slew of crises from war to inflation push global warming down the list of priorities for world governments.

"Each country has a view. Every country has a voice. Getting agreement on every word, every sentence is tough but vital work," Simon Stiell told the summit.

"There is no collective success without compromise from every party. As we head into the second ?week, I urge parties to move swiftly to the hardest issues and to avoid tactical delays."

Big fossil fuel producers and consumers at the talks are resisting any deal that would specify firm new targets or a shift away from oil, gas and coal, observers said, posing a challenge for summit host Turkey and lead negotiator Australia to land ?the kind of ambitious agreement climate advocates say is needed to address global warming.

A UN report last month found the world is already on course to exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warming threshold, a limit scientists say should prevent the worst effects of climate change.

Australia's COP31 President of Negotiations Chris Bowen said he expected a first draft of a deal text to emerge early next week.

headline: Oil holds in tight range as Gulf attacks sustain risk premium
body:
Brent ‌crude down 47 cents to $92.10 a barrel by 12:38pm PKT. US WTI futures down 43 cents to $82.98 a barrel

Oil prices in Asian trade changed little on Monday as investors priced in a risk premium from persistent shipping and refinery attacks in the Middle East, amid diplomatic efforts to end the war.

Brent ‌crude futures fell 47 cents, or 0.51%, to $92.10 a barrel by 12:38pm PKT. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) futures were down 43 cents, or 0.52%, to $82.98 a barrel. Brent crude rose to a session high of $93.12 earlier in ​the day, while US WTI climbed to $83.95.

Brent declined 4% last week and WTI 5%.

The ​fighting from the unresolved US-Israeli war on Iran continues to support oil prices, ⁠however. On Sunday, the Houthi movement claimed it attacked a Saudi Arabian oil refinery, while ​the UK Maritime Trade Operations reported multiple attacks on shipping in the Gulf and near the Strait of ​Hormuz over the weekend.

"A tense US-Iran stalemate increasingly looks like the base case through year-end, but Trump can still flip-flop over the prospect of renewed military action," said Vandana Hari, founder of oil market analysis provider Vanda ​Insights.

"The ebb and flow of threats and harsher rhetoric from Washington and Tehran will likely continue ​to drive the marginal geopolitical risk premium in crude, while keeping prices broadly rangebound unless either side takes ‌more ⁠concrete steps towards escalation," Hari said.

headline: Attacks on shipping near Strait of Hormuz hit wartime high in October: UK maritime monitor
body:
Over 30 incidents in October, at least 22 recorded in November as shipping traffic remains 65% below prewar levels

Attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz reached their highest monthly level in October since the US-Iran conflict began in late February, according to official figures from the UK Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO).

Incidents reported to UKMTO surpassed 30 in October for the first time since the outbreak of the war, while at least 22 attacks were recorded in November as of Sunday across the Strait of Hormuz, the Gulf, and the Gulf of Oman.

Before October, reported attacks averaged roughly 10 per month, according to the data. Separate figures from the International Maritime Organisation also indicate that October saw the highest number of confirmed incidents so far this year.

Read: Iran says it will use all available tools to confront US naval blockade

In its weekly overview published on Friday, UKMTO said its figures only reflect incidents verified through primary sources, noting that additional incidents are known but cannot be independently verified.

The agency also said in mid-October that the majority of attacked vessels were declining to report incidents, while many ships have switched off tracking devices to avoid detection.

Commercial traffic through the strait, which carried roughly one-fifth of global oil supplies before the war, remains about 65% below pre-conflict levels following Iran's efforts to halt shipping and a US blockade on Iranian ports.

headline: Cyberattacks on US ports and cargo ships surge, with thousands of daily attempts
body:
Hackers linked to gangs, hostile states target ports, tankers as AI raises fears of faster exploitation of weaknesses

United States ports and cargo vessels are facing an intensifying wave of cyberattacks, with hackers launching thousands of attempts daily to infiltrate critical infrastructure underpinning global trade.

The number and sophistication of attacks have risen sharply in recent months, with ports, oil tankers, and major shipping companies increasingly coming under threat from cybercriminals and groups linked to hostile states.

Executives at the Port of Corpus Christi in Texas, the largest US crude oil export hub, told the Financial Times that their networks face hundreds, and sometimes thousands, of hacking attempts every day.

The port, which handles approximately 2.3 million barrels of crude oil exports daily, has become a target for hackers seeking to breach its systems and gain access by deceiving employees.

His reign was eventually ended in 1921 by Cuban genius Jose Raul Capablanca, whose legendary endgame technique is still studied. And he won the World championship at home, in Havana, beating Lasker rather convincingly.

The reigning champion, in fact, conceded defeat with 10 still to be played; he had lost four games, won none and drawn 10.

The match was scheduled to resume after a rest of a few days, but Lasker’s remark in Latin translated to: “Thus passes the glory of the world.”

Capablanca’s glory as the World champion didn’t last long, though. He failed to defend his title in the 1927 match against Alexander Alekhine, the Moscow-born French player whose attacking imaginative style has many admirers, including Garry Kasparov.

Alekhine defended his crown, beating Efim Bogoljubow twice, in 1929 and 1934. He, however, lost his title in 1935 to Max Euwe, the Dutch mathematician who would go on to become a professor of computer science.

Alekhine had his revenge though, beating Euwe in 1937 to start his second reign as the World champion. When he passed away in 1946, he was still the World champion. Nobody else has had that honour.

Between the export controls that began during the first Trump term and now, there has been a significant change in the technology and business of semiconductors. Image for representation only | Photo Credit: Getty Images/iStockphoto

The story so far: The battle for the most-sought-after commodity that underpins development of artificial intelligence technology just grew fiercer. On November 16, the U.S. Commerce Department issued an interim final rule (IFR) requiring companies to have licences to supply advanced American AI chips to data centre operators outside the U.S. with substantial computing power to businesses headquartered in two dozen countries, including China, Iran, and Russia. The interim rule came just days ahead of the meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China on the sidelines of the November 18-19 APEC Summit.

headline: Healthcare AI: hospitals lack capacity to measure real-world patient outcomes, warns French expert
body:
Updated - November 22, 2026 09:15 am IST - Bengaluru

A system achieving 95% accuracy against a doctor’s 90% might not necessarily perform better in clinical settings. | Photo Credit: Reuters

Hospitals worldwide are ill-equipped to assess whether artificial intelligence (AI) systems deployed in their facilities actually improve patient outcomes, raising questions about the clinical and economic value of healthcare AI, Emmanuel Bacry, Scientific Director of France’s Health Data Hub, said at the Bengaluru Tech Summit.

“There are maybe six or seven hospitals in the whole world today that are able to evaluate medical devices deployed in their system,” Mr. Bacry said. Hospitals struggle to access and integrate patient information to track outcomes after discharge, including recovery rates and mortality, making it difficult to establish the actual impact of AI-based medical technologies.

“In hospitals, we don’t know how to compute that,” he said, referring to the return on investment of such technologies. “So imagine now, if they adopt AI.”

Mr. Bacry cited an alert system based on rules-based AI, or an expert system, designed to warn intensive care unit (ICU) staff about severe kidney failure. Despite functioning effectively, the system was associated with a doubling of deaths in two of the six US hospitals where it was deployed in 2022, he said. He did not identify the study.

While researchers had offered hypotheses, the precise cause remained unknown. Mr. Bacry suggested that the absence of a tested response protocol among hospital personnel could have contributed to the outcome.

“In hospitals, we don’t know how to compute that,” he said, referring to the return on investment of such technologies. “So imagine now, if they adopt AI.”

Mr. Bacry cited an alert system based on rules-based AI, or an expert system, designed to warn intensive care unit (ICU) staff about severe kidney failure. Despite functioning effectively, the system was associated with a doubling of deaths in two of the six US hospitals where it was deployed in 2022, he said. He did not identify the study.

While researchers had offered hypotheses, the precise cause remained unknown. Mr. Bacry suggested that the absence of a tested response protocol among hospital personnel could have contributed to the outcome.

“We just replaced the alert done by a human with the alert done by the medical device. And that changes the whole thing,” he said, underlining the importance of integrating AI into clinical workflows rather than treating it as a standalone technology.

He also cautioned against evaluating diagnostic AI tools solely through laboratory accuracy scores or comparisons with doctors. A system achieving 95% accuracy against a doctor’s 90% might not necessarily perform better in clinical settings. “When you deploy in real life, you can forget about these scores,” he said.

Mr. Bacry flagged another concern: AI systems can identify patterns that even their developers cannot explain. Citing research, he said one model predicted ethnicity from chest X-rays with approximately 85% accuracy, while another inferred sex from eye images with 95% accuracy.

Such hidden correlations could influence medical decisions without clinicians understanding the underlying basis, potentially introducing unintended bias into diagnosis and treatment.

In a separate interaction with The Hindu, Mr. Bacry warned that healthcare AI development was heavily skewed towards Western populations. By his estimate, nearly 70% of global healthcare AI training data came from male, white and Western populations.

“We are developing an Occidental AI and even narrow types of Occidental AI,” he said.

He advocated smaller, locally tailored AI models trained on representative population data, arguing that deploying large, general-purpose models without adaptation could have disastrous consequences, particularly in developing countries.

Mr. Bacry heads the Health Data Hub, established under French law in 2019 to facilitate secondary use of health data for research. He is also a research director at France’s National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) at Université Paris Dauphine–PSL.

headline: In Keralam, the children beyond healthcare
body:
Updated - November 22, 2026 04:48 pm IST

In Attappady, a predominantly tribal area of Palakkad district in Keralam, a mother soothes her baby. | Photo Credit: Sakeer Hussain

Between the pages of a logbook recording Dakshina’s treatment are ₹100, ₹50, ₹20, and ₹10 notes. Dakshina’s mother, Minnal Rani, had filed them away for her daughter’s medical expenses. The child is gone, but the money remains untouched. “We will never spend it,” she says, fighting back tears.

Dakshina was five months old when doctors detected a hole in her heart. Born on June 13, 2025, she was taken to many hospitals, including one in Thiruvananthapuram, Keralam’s capital. With surgery ruled out, she was eventually referred to a cooperative hospital at Perinthalmanna, in Malappuram district, a two-and-a-half-hour drive away from home. She died here, on April 13, 2026.

Rani and her husband Chandra Sekhar say the hospital refused to release their daughter’s body until they paid a bill of ₹10,000. They managed to raise the money with the help of a ward councillor.

“We buried her under that tree,” says Rani, pointing to a coconut tree near their house at Vechapathi hamlet in Sholayur panchayat of Attappadi, Palakkad district.

headline: How did the COP31 climate agreement fall apart – and what happens now?
body:
Updated - November 23, 2026 01:13 pm IST

For many observers, the litmus test for success at COP31 was whether countries could make any headway on the root cause of climate change – fossil fuels. Unfortunately, fossil fuels proved unmentionable. File photo | Photo Credit: AP

Two days after the COP31 global climate summit was supposed to finish, the talks in Antalya, Turkey, have come to an end – but not as we might have hoped.

Agreement simply could not be reached. The sticking point was the omission of fossil fuels in draft texts. The European Union led a revolt, shattering the consensus needed to adopt the cover text proposed by the Turkish and Australian conveners.

In a year of unprecedented climate disasters, a supercharged El Niño and as the world heads inevitably past 1.5 °C of warming, the EU and other nations said that the international process did not meet the moment.

Some coverage has suggested the rejection of the cover text is a sign the entire summit was a failure. This isn’t quite right.

These texts have always been add-ons to the formal negotiation process. Countries have regularly agreed these political, overarching statements, particularly since the Glasgow meeting in 2021, but they are not a requirement.

Its failure does not signal the end of the COP process – or the breakdown of the Paris Agreement. What it may mean is that international climate cooperation will look different from this point onwards.

Updated - November 23, 2026 01:13 pm IST

For many observers, the litmus test for success at COP31 was whether countries could make any headway on the root cause of climate change – fossil fuels. Unfortunately, fossil fuels proved unmentionable. File photo | Photo Credit: AP

Two days after the COP31 global climate summit was supposed to finish, the talks in Antalya, Turkey, have come to an end – but not as we might have hoped.

Agreement simply could not be reached. The sticking point was the omission of fossil fuels in draft texts. The European Union led a revolt, shattering the consensus needed to adopt the cover text proposed by the Turkish and Australian conveners.

In a year of unprecedented climate disasters, a supercharged El Niño and as the world heads inevitably past 1.5 °C of warming, the EU and other nations said that the international process did not meet the moment.

Some coverage has suggested the rejection of the cover text is a sign the entire summit was a failure. This isn’t quite right.

These texts have always been add-ons to the formal negotiation process. Countries have regularly agreed these political, overarching statements, particularly since the Glasgow meeting in 2021, but they are not a requirement.

Its failure does not signal the end of the COP process – or the breakdown of the Paris Agreement. What it may mean is that international climate cooperation will look different from this point onwards.

For many observers, the litmus test for success at COP31 was whether countries could make any headway on the root cause of climate change – fossil fuels. Unfortunately, fossil fuels proved unmentionable.

Three years ago at COP28 in Dubai, countries agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels”, marking the first time fossil fuels had explicitly been mentioned in an official decision text in decades of negotiations.

The Dubai text was hailed as “the beginning of the end of the fossil fuel era”. But there was little sign that hope would be realised in Turkey.

In a repeat of last year’s fraught negotiations at COP30 in Brazil, major fossil fuel producing nations Saudi Arabia and Russia banded together to block any reference in the negotiating outcomes and proposed cover text.

Australia and Turkey proposed a compromise – no fossil fuel language in exchange for support for electrification “with the greatest possible use of clean energy”.

This seemed to get Saudi Arabia over the line but drew backlash from the European Union, Panama, the Marshall Islands, Vanuatu, and Belize, who rejected the cover text.

Brazil took a different approach to the same problem last year. In a bid to break the deadlock, Brazil committed to develop a global strategy to phase out fossil fuels outside the formal negotiating agenda.

The roadmap was launched at this year’s summit in Turkey and managed to attract support from big fossil fuel producers such as India, Germany and Nigeria. Countries across the European Union are launching similar roadmaps.

Frustration over fossil fuels at COP31 is likely to lead more nations to go outside official talks to progress phase-out efforts. Earlier this year, 57 nations attended the first conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels in Santa Marta, Colombia. Another meeting is planned for next year, co-hosted by Tuvalu and Ireland.

Neither the Turkish hosts nor their Australian partners seemed keen to mention fossil fuels. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan was untroubled by the optics of announcing two huge new oilfields in Turkey in his speech at the summit opening. While Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese highlighted the existential risks to Pacific countries from climate change, he made no commitment to stop approving new Australian coal and gas projects.

Both leaders much preferred to talk about electrification, namely the flagship “35 by 35” electrification pledge. The goal here is to boost electricity’s share of final energy use globally from around 23% at present to 35% by 2035.

Efforts to embed this goal in the cover text failed. But the electrification pledge drew strong support outside official negotiations. More than 75 countries and 180 businesses signed on, including the European Union and China.

This year’s climate summit was billed as an “implementation COP”, focused on delivering the pledges countries had already made to address climate change.

Overseen by Australia in its role as “president of negotiations”, the formal talks largely focused on the actions countries are taking to reduce emissions and adapt to climate change, whether their response is sufficiently urgent and whether funds aimed at supporting the most vulnerable countries are adequate.

It was abundantly obvious that longstanding divisions had not been overcome. Developed countries called for emissions to be cut faster, while developing countries responded by pointing to a lack of financial support to do so.

African countries, in particular, stressed that an “implementation COP” was meaningless if rich nations failed to provide the actual resources needed to act.

Despite the general gloom, these talks did achieve progress in a few areas. Nations moved forwards on supporting a just transition (shifting to clean energy fairly) via a “phased approach”, as well as improving alignment in climate adaptation, which will help the poorest nations to implement their adaptation plans.

But broader efforts to find a way forward on the Paris Agreement’s Global Goal on Adaptation were left unresolved.

Decisions stalled in many negotiating rooms in the face of hard “red lines” declared by different blocs of countries.

Countries failed to reach any agreement on the vital question of cutting emissions, after Saudia Arabia and Russia blocked a proposed decision. Both are among the world’s top fossil fuel exporting nations.

This failure has left the world without any dedicated negotiating process on cutting emissions under the Paris Agreement. It’s possible nations could agree to renew a work program on climate mitigation at next year’s COP32 talks in Ethiopia.

Who pays for the costs of climate change has long been a contentious point. Developing countries face the brunt of damage from climate change, but have emitted far less – and have much less money to spend on adaptation.

Ahead of COP31, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said talks on new climate finance commitments were “dead in the water”. He urged delegates to focus on implementing existing pledges rather than try for fresh funding.

The summit failed to meet even these low expectations. No concrete progress was achieved on the goal of tripling funds for climate adaptation pledged last year at COP30 in Brazil.

Ahead of the summit, the Australian government flagged the need to boost global contributions to the official Pacific climate fund.

This, too, didn’t eventuate. Rich nations – including Australia – merely re-announced their existing pledges, leaving the Pacific fund A$450 million short of its 2026 target of $749 million.

Ironically, the most notable pledge came from the Solomon Islands, a small Pacific nation. Prime Minister Matthew Wale pledged $600,000 to the global Green Climate Fund. “The Pacific did not create this crisis,” he declared. “But we will not stand by and wait for others to act”.

A few new commitments arrived by the end of the two week summit from nations such as Canada and Norway.

Unusually, climate science was front and centre at COP31.

This year, a small bloc of fossil fuel-producing countries has been obstructing the publication of key scientific reports from the world’s leading body of climate scientists, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change.

This year marks the first UN summit since it was officially confirmed the world will overshoot the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C goal by 2030.

With the collapse of support for the cover text, statements supporting release of the latest climate science didn’t get approval. All that remained were technical conclusions which “expressed utmost concern” that climate impacts will continue to increase with every increment of global warming.

COP31 gave Australia a unique global role. After being outmanoeuvred in their bid to host the summit, Australia secured a role in overseeing negotiations.

Australian Climate and Energy Minister Chris Bowen and his team had the unenviable task of seeking consensus between 195 countries and the European Union.

After the cover text was rejected, Bowen declared Australia had left “nothing on the field” but had faced “unbridgeable red lines.”

Hours beforehand, Fijian Climate Minister Lynda Tabuya acknowledged Bowen’s efforts, noting the failure was “not yours to carry […] it is the responsibility of all parties.”

This year’s climate summit took the unenviable record of the longest ever. With consensus seemingly impossible, some civil society representatives dubbed it “the worst COP ever.”

Outgoing UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres blamed “powerful fossil fuel interests”, including fossil fuel exporters and corporate lobbyists.

Some nations are now calling for urgent reform to negotiations long paralysed by vetoes and disconnected from science.

Unfortunately, any change to official voting processes would itself require a consensus decision.

Consensus is hard to achieve, but powerful. The power of the Paris Agreement draws on the fact it represents the view of nearly every country – big or small, rich or poor.

COP31 President Murat Kurum began the summit expressing hopes this year’s talks would leave a legacy of “working together.”

That was a false hope. A more realistic hope is that the collapse of consensus may be the shock the world needs to change course.

As former UN climate chief Christiana Figueres has said, we should not see the refusal of more than 130 countries to sign an inadequate deal as a failure. Rather, it might be “a sign of courage”.
